sections.title: Average vs Instantaneous Rate

board_events.text: Rate: how fast $[A]$ changes with time

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="300" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="60" y1="30" x2="60" y2="250" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="250" x2="430" y2="250" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><text x="18" y="140" fill="#111111" font-size="13" transform="rotate(-90 18 140)">[A] / mol L⁻¹</text><text x="230" y="285" fill="#111111" font-size="13">time / s</text><path d="M75,55 C150,120 210,180 300,215 C350,232 400,240 420,243" fill="none" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="120" cy="95" r="4" fill="#d1242f"/><circle cx="300" cy="215" r="4" fill="#d1242f"/><line x1="120" y1="95" x2="300" y2="215" stroke="#d1242f" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text x="150" y="150" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12">average rate</text><text x="150" y="165" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12">= slope of secant</text><circle cx="210" cy="167" r="4" fill="#1a7f37"/><line x1="150" y1="120" x2="290" y2="222" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="300" y="150" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12">instantaneous</text><text x="300" y="165" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12">= slope of tangent</text><text x="196" y="192" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12">t</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Concentration-time curve: average rate is the secant slope, instantaneous rate the tangent slope

board_events.text: Average rate = change in concentration over a whole time interval.
Instantaneous rate = slope of the tangent at a single moment.
Reactant $[A]$ falls, so $d[A]/dt$ is negative — add a minus sign to keep the rate positive.
Products grow, so their derivatives are already positive.

segments.text: Picture yourself on the foot-over-bridge at a busy railway station, watching the ticket queue below. There are two very different questions here. How many tickets sell over the whole morning is one thing. How fast tickets are moving right this second is another. Chemical reactions behave in exactly the same way.

This curve shows a reactant concentration falling with time. The red dashed line joining two points is the average rate over that stretch. The green line just kissing the curve at one point is the instantaneous rate at that instant. Same reaction, two different speeds.
The average rate is simply the change in concentration divided by the time interval it happened over. It is the morning total divided by the morning hours.
Written out, the average rate equals minus delta A over a delta t, or plus delta C over c delta t. We will explain those coefficients in a moment.
The instantaneous rate is the speed at one precise clock reading, which spikes when a train is announced and crawls during a lull. Mathematically it is the slope of the tangent.
In symbols it is minus one over a, d A by d t, equal to plus one over c, d C by d t. The derivative captures that this very moment.
Here is the sign subtlety. A reactant is disappearing, so its concentration is shrinking and its derivative is negative. We slap a minus sign in front so the rate we quote comes out positive.
Products are being made, so their concentration rises and their derivative is already positive. No extra minus sign needed there.

सोचिए आप एक busy railway station के foot-over-bridge पर खड़े हैं और नीचे ticket queue देख रहे हैं। यहाँ दो अलग-अलग सवाल हैं। पूरी सुबह में कितनी tickets बिकीं, ये एक बात है। और अभी इसी second में tickets कितनी तेज़ी से move कर रही हैं, ये बिलकुल अलग बात है। Chemical reactions भी exactly ऐसे ही behave करती हैं।

ये curve दिखाता है कि reactant की concentration time के साथ गिर रही है। लाल dashed line जो दो points को जोड़ती है, वो average rate है। हरी line जो curve को एक point पर छूती है, वो instantaneous rate है। एक ही reaction, पर दो अलग speeds।
Average rate बस concentration के change को time interval से divide करना है। यानी सुबह का total बँटा सुबह के घंटों से।
Formula में, average rate बराबर होता है minus delta A over a delta t, या plus delta C over c delta t. इन coefficients को हम अभी थोड़ी देर में समझाएँगे।
Instantaneous rate वो speed है जो एक precise clock reading पर होती है — train announce होते ही spike करती है और lull में धीमी पड़ जाती है। Mathematically ये tangent का slope है।
Symbols में ये है minus one over a, d A by d t, equal to plus one over c, d C by d t. Derivative इसी exact moment को capture करता है।
अब एक subtle बात। Reactant disappear हो रहा है, तो उसकी concentration घट रही है और derivative negative है। इसलिए हम आगे एक minus sign लगाते हैं ताकि rate positive आए।
Products बन रहे हैं, तो उनकी concentration बढ़ती है और derivative पहले से ही positive है। वहाँ कोई extra minus sign नहीं चाहिए।

sections.title: One Rate for the Whole Reaction

board_events.text: Why divide by the stoichiometric coefficient?

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="300" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="28" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃</text><text x="70" y="70" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">N₂ (÷1)</text><rect x="45" y="80" width="50" height="30" fill="#1f6feb"/><text x="70" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">1×</text><text x="200" y="70" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">H₂ (÷3)</text><rect x="150" y="80" width="100" height="30" fill="#d1242f"/><text x="200" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">3× faster</text><text x="345" y="70" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">NH₃ (÷2)</text><rect x="310" y="80" width="70" height="30" fill="#1a7f37"/><text x="345" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">2× formed</text><rect x="60" y="165" width="340" height="70" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#8c959f"/><text x="230" y="195" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">Divide each by its coefficient</text><text x="230" y="220" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">→ one agreed "line speed" = Rate</text><text x="230" y="265" fill="#9a6700" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">like plating thalis: rotis used 3× the dal, but one line-rate</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Species change at different numerical speeds; dividing by coefficients gives one agreed rate

board_events.text: For $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3$, hydrogen vanishes three times faster than nitrogen.
So the three species do NOT change at the same numerical speed.
Divide each species' rate by its coefficient to get ONE agreed number.
Think of plating thalis: rotis are used three times as fast as the dal, but the line speed is a single figure.

segments.text: Here is the bit that trips up half the class. We want one single number that everybody agrees to call the rate of the reaction, even though different species change at different speeds.

Look at this picture. For nitrogen plus three hydrogen giving two ammonia, one nitrogen molecule vanishes, three hydrogens vanish, and two ammonia molecules appear. The bars show they move at genuinely different numerical speeds.
For every one molecule of nitrogen that disappears, three of hydrogen disappear. So hydrogen drops three times faster than nitrogen.
That means if you just read off the raw rate of change, the three species give you three different numbers. That cannot be the reaction's rate.

The fix is to divide each species' rate by its stoichiometric coefficient. Rate equals minus d N two by d t, equals minus one third d H two by d t, equals plus one half d N H three by d t. Now all three agree.
So always divide by the coefficient. Forgetting this factor and equating the raw rates is one of the most common slips in this chapter.

<chuckle> Think of a thali assembly line at a wedding kitchen. One thali needs one bowl of dal, three rotis, and produces two sweets. The rotis get consumed three times as fast as the dal, but the line speed, thalis per minute, is one agreed number.
अब वो बात जहाँ आधी class अटक जाती है। हमें एक single number चाहिए जिसे सब मिलकर reaction का rate कहें, जबकि अलग-अलग species अलग speeds पर change होती हैं।

इस picture को देखिए। N two plus three H two giving two N H three में, एक N two molecule गायब होता है, तीन H two गायब होते हैं, और दो N H three बनते हैं। Bars दिखाती हैं कि ये सच में अलग numerical speeds पर चलते हैं।
हर एक N two molecule के गायब होने पर तीन H two गायब होते हैं। मतलब hydrogen, nitrogen से तीन गुना तेज़ गिरता है।
इसका मतलब अगर आप raw rate of change पढ़ें, तो तीनों species तीन अलग numbers देंगी। ये reaction का rate नहीं हो सकता।

Fix ये है कि हर species के rate को उसके stoichiometric coefficient से divide करो। Rate equals minus d N two by d t, equals minus one third d H two by d t, equals plus one half d N H three by d t. अब तीनों agree करते हैं।
तो हमेशा coefficient से divide करो। ये factor भूलना और raw rates को बराबर मान लेना इस chapter की सबसे common गलतियों में से एक है।

<chuckle> एक wedding kitchen की thali assembly line सोचिए। एक thali के लिए एक bowl दाल, तीन रोटी चाहिए और दो मिठाइयाँ बनती हैं। रोटियाँ दाल से तीन गुना तेज़ खर्च होती हैं, पर line speed, यानी thalis per minute, एक ही agreed number है।

sections.title: Rate Law, Order & Molecularity

board_events.text: What actually controls the rate?

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="300" fill="#ffffff"/><rect x="30" y="40" width="180" height="220" rx="10" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="250" y="40" width="180" height="220" rx="10" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="120" y="68" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">ORDER</text><text x="120" y="90" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">observed</text><text x="120" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">from experiment</text><text x="120" y="160" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">may be 0,</text><text x="120" y="180" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">fraction, or</text><text x="120" y="200" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">negative</text><text x="120" y="235" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">any reaction</text><text x="340" y="68" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">MOLECULARITY</text><text x="340" y="90" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">mechanistic</text><text x="340" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">counted species</text><text x="340" y="160" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">whole number</text><text x="340" y="180" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">1, 2, or 3</text><text x="340" y="200" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">never 0 / fraction</text><text x="340" y="235" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">elementary steps only</text><text x="230" y="285" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Order is observed, molecularity is mechanistic</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Order is observed from experiment; molecularity is a counted mechanistic quantity

board_events.text: Experiment — and only experiment — gives the rate law.
$x$ and $y$ are found in the lab; you CANNOT read them off the balanced equation.
Molecularity = number of species that physically collide in one elementary step.
Order may be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a whole number 1, 2 or 3.
Molecularity is defined only for elementary steps; for a complex reaction it is meaningless.

segments.text: <curious> So what actually controls the rate? Not the balanced equation, as tempting as that is. Experiment, and only experiment, tells us how rate depends on concentration.

This contrast is the heart of the subtopic. On the left, order: observed, experimental, and it can be zero, a fraction, or even negative. On the right, molecularity: counted, mechanistic, always a whole number.
We find, in the lab, that rate usually depends on reactant concentrations raised to certain powers. That experimentally observed relationship is the rate law.
We write rate equals k times A to the power x times B to the power y. The sum x plus y is the order of the reaction, and k is the rate constant.
Crucially, x and y are measured, not derived. A balanced equation is bookkeeping for atoms, not a stopwatch for speed. You cannot read the exponents off it.
Sitting right next to order is its frequently confused cousin, molecularity. Molecularity is the number of reactant species that physically collide in a single elementary step.
Keep them apart. Order comes from experiment and may be zero, fractional, or negative. Molecularity is a counted whole number, one, two, or three, and never zero or a fraction.
And molecularity is defined only for an elementary reaction that happens in one shot. For a multi step complex reaction, an overall molecularity is meaningless, because each step has its own.
<curious> तो असल में rate को control क्या करता है? Balanced equation नहीं, चाहे वो कितना ही tempting लगे। Experiment, और सिर्फ़ experiment बताता है कि rate concentration पर कैसे depend करता है।
ये contrast इस subtopic का दिल है। बाईं तरफ़ order: observed, experimental, और ये zero, fraction, या negative भी हो सकता है। दाईं तरफ़ molecularity: counted, mechanistic, हमेशा whole number।
हम lab में पाते हैं कि rate आमतौर पर reactant concentrations पर कुछ powers के साथ depend करता है। यही experimentally observed relationship rate law है।
हम लिखते हैं rate equals k times A to the power x times B to the power y. इनका sum, x plus y, reaction का order है, और k rate constant है।
बहुत ज़रूरी बात — x और y measured होते हैं, derived नहीं। Balanced equation atoms का bookkeeping है, speed का stopwatch नहीं। आप exponents उससे नहीं पढ़ सकते।
Order के ठीक बगल में उसका frequently confused cousin है, molecularity. Molecularity उन reactant species की संख्या है जो single elementary step में physically collide करती हैं।
इन दोनों को अलग रखिए। Order experiment से आता है और zero, fractional, या negative हो सकता है। Molecularity एक counted whole number है — एक, दो या तीन — और कभी zero या fraction नहीं।
और molecularity सिर्फ़ उस elementary reaction के लिए defined है जो एक ही shot में होती है। Multi-step complex reaction के लिए overall molecularity meaningless है, क्योंकि हर step का अपना होता है।

sections.title: Extracting the Rate Law from Initial-Rate Data

board_events.text: The isolate-one-variable method

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="300" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="28" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Isolate one variable</text><rect x="40" y="50" width="170" height="60" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#8c959f"/><text x="125" y="75" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">Exp 1 → Exp 2</text><text x="125" y="95" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">[A] doubles, [B] fixed</text><rect x="250" y="50" width="170" height="60" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#8c959f"/><text x="335" y="75" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">Exp 1 → Exp 3</text><text x="335" y="95" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">[B] triples, [A] fixed</text><text x="125" y="150" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">rate ×2 ⇒ 2 = 2ₓ</text><text x="125" y="172" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">x = 1</text><text x="335" y="150" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">rate ×9 ⇒ 9 = 3ʸ</text><text x="335" y="172" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">y = 2</text><rect x="120" y="205" width="220" height="55" rx="8" fill="#fff8c5" stroke="#9a6700"/><text x="230" y="230" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">Overall order = x + y</text><text x="230" y="250" fill="#d1242f" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">= 3</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Change one concentration at a time; read each exponent from the rate ratio

board_events.text: Step 1: across two experiments, change ONE reactant while holding the others fixed.
Step 2: solve for the exponent, often by inspection.
Doubling that doubles rate gives $x=1$; doubling that quadruples rate gives $x=2$.
Step 3: repeat for each reactant, then sum the exponents for the overall order.
Step 4: back-substitute one experiment to get $k$ — and check its units.

segments.text: The examinable skill here is a clean procedure: pull the rate law straight out of initial-rate data. It rests on one idea, controlling variables.
Follow the picture. On the left we compare two experiments where A doubles but B is held fixed, and the rate doubles. On the right, B triples while A is fixed, and the rate goes up ninefold.

Step one: change one reactant's concentration while holding the others fixed. If two things change at once, you cannot attribute the rate change to either, the same logic as any controlled experiment.
Step two, form the ratio. Rate two over rate one equals the concentration ratio raised to the power x, the order with respect to that reactant.
Now solve for x, usually just by looking. Doubling the concentration and watching what the rate does tells you the exponent directly.
The shortcut: doubling that doubles the rate means x is one. Doubling that quadruples the rate means x is two. No algebra needed.
Step three, repeat the trick for each reactant, then add the exponents to get the overall order. Here one plus two gives an overall order of three.
Step four, put any single experiment's numbers back into rate equals k A to the x B to the y, solve for k, and report its units. Those units double as a check on your order.
यहाँ examinable skill एक clean procedure है: initial-rate data से rate law को सीधे निकालना। ये एक ही idea पर टिका है — controlling variables।

Picture follow कीजिए। बाईं तरफ़ हम दो experiments compare करते हैं जहाँ A double होता है पर B fixed है, और rate double हो जाता है। दाईं तरफ़ B triple होता है जबकि A fixed है, और rate नौ गुना बढ़ जाता है।
Step one: एक reactant की concentration change करो और बाकी fixed रखो। अगर दो चीज़ें एक साथ बदलें, तो आप rate change का कारण किसी एक को नहीं दे सकते — यही logic किसी भी controlled experiment का है।
Step two, ratio बनाओ। Rate two over rate one बराबर है concentration ratio raised to the power x, जो उस reactant के respect में order है।
अब x solve करो, अक्सर बस देखकर। Concentration को double करके rate क्या करता है, ये सीधे exponent बता देता है।
Shortcut ये है: double करने पर rate double हो तो x एक है। Double करने पर rate चार गुना हो तो x दो है। कोई algebra नहीं चाहिए।
Step three, हर reactant के लिए यही trick दोहराओ, फिर exponents जोड़कर overall order निकालो। यहाँ एक plus two देता है overall order तीन।
Step four, किसी एक experiment के numbers rate equals k A to the x B to the y में वापस डालो, k solve करो, और उसकी units report करो। वो units आपके order का check भी बन जाती हैं।

sections.title: Order vs Molecularity in Multi-Step Reactions

board_events.text: Order from a mechanism

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="300" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="26" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">The slowest step throttles the whole chain</text><rect x="40" y="90" width="110" height="60" fill="#1a7f37" opacity="0.85"/><text x="95" y="125" fill="#ffffff" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">FAST</text><text x="95" y="170" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">Step 1 (equilibrium)</text><rect x="150" y="112" width="120" height="16" fill="#d1242f"/><text x="210" y="100" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">SLOW = bottleneck</text><text x="210" y="170" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">Step 2 (rate-determining)</text><rect x="270" y="90" width="110" height="60" fill="#1a7f37" opacity="0.85"/><text x="325" y="125" fill="#ffffff" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">FAST</text><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="410" y2="120" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3" opacity="0.4"/><polygon points="410,110 430,120 410,130" fill="#333333"/><rect x="60" y="205" width="340" height="60" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#8c959f"/><text x="230" y="230" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">Rate set by slow step — but if it holds an</text><text x="230" y="250" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">intermediate, substitute it out first</text></svg>
board_events.caption: A chain runs at the speed of its slowest link; substitute out any intermediate

board_events.text: For an elementary step: order = molecularity = sum of coefficients in that step.
For a complex reaction: find the rate-determining (slowest) step — the bottleneck.
Write the rate using the slow step's species.
If a slow-step species is a fast-formed intermediate, substitute it out using the pre-equilibrium.
Board shortcut: 'order = molecularity of the slowest step' — TRUE only when no intermediate is substituted.
The moment an intermediate is substituted, overall order can exceed the slow step's molecularity.

segments.text: Now the deeper case: how do you get the order when the reaction runs through several steps, a mechanism?
The mental image is a chain, or a kitchen line. It runs only as fast as its slowest link. Here two fast steps sandwich one slow step, and the slow one is the bottleneck.

First, the easy situation. For a genuinely elementary step, the order equals the molecularity equals the sum of the coefficients in that step. This is the only time the balanced equation hands you the rate law directly.
For a complex reaction, locate the rate-determining step, the slowest one. It throttles everything downstream, so it sets the overall rate.
Write the rate in terms of the species in that slow step. That is your starting expression for the rate law.
But watch for a trap. If one of those slow-step species is a reactive intermediate, formed in a fast step, you cannot leave it in. Replace it using the fast pre-equilibrium step.
There is a board-level shortcut that says order equals the molecularity of the slowest step. That is true only when the slow step contains no fast-equilibrium intermediate to substitute.
<whisper> The moment you must substitute an intermediate, the overall order can exceed the slow step's molecularity. That is exactly the J E E Advanced trap coming up in the last worked example.
अब गहरा case: जब reaction कई steps से गुज़रती है, यानी mechanism, तब order कैसे निकालें?
Mental image एक chain या kitchen line है। ये सिर्फ़ अपने सबसे slow link जितनी तेज़ चलती है। यहाँ दो fast steps एक slow step को sandwich करते हैं, और वही slow step bottleneck है।
पहले आसान situation। एक genuinely elementary step के लिए order equals molecularity equals उस step के coefficients का sum. यही एकमात्र time है जब balanced equation सीधे rate law देती है।
Complex reaction के लिए rate-determining step ढूँढो, यानी सबसे slow वाला। वही downstream सब कुछ throttle करता है, तो वही overall rate set करता है।
Rate को उस slow step की species के terms में लिखो। यही आपकी rate law की starting expression है।
पर एक trap का ध्यान रखो। अगर उन slow-step species में से कोई reactive intermediate है, जो किसी fast step में बना है, तो उसे छोड़ नहीं सकते। उसे fast pre-equilibrium step से replace करो।
एक board-level shortcut कहता है order equals molecularity of the slowest step. ये तभी सच है जब slow step में कोई fast-equilibrium intermediate substitute न करना पड़े।
<whisper> जिस पल आपको intermediate substitute करना पड़ता है, overall order slow step की molecularity से ज़्यादा हो सकता है। यही आगे आने वाले J E E Advanced example का trap है।

sections.title: The Rate Constant and Its Order-Dependent Units

board_events.text: The rate constant $k$ and its units
$k$ is the value of the rate when every reactant concentration equals unity.
Three properties: $k$ is concentration-independent, temperature-dependent, and a larger $k$ means a faster reaction.

board_events.caption: Units of k for each order, from the general formula

board_events.text: Order zero gives mol per litre per second; order one gives per second; order two gives litre per mole per second.
Reading the units is a free check on your computed order.

segments.text: Let us pin down the rate constant, k, sometimes called the specific reaction rate. It is the value the rate takes when every reactant concentration equals one.
The definition follows from rate equals k times concentration terms: set all concentrations to unity and the rate is simply k.
Memorise its three defining properties. k does not depend on concentration, it does depend on temperature, and a larger k means a faster reaction.

Now the diagnostic worth memorising. Since k equals rate divided by concentration to the power n, its units are mol per litre, all raised to one minus n, times per second. That tidies to mol to the one minus n, litre to the n minus one, per second.
This table just plugs each order into that formula. Notice the units genuinely change with the order, which is what makes them useful.
For order zero, k is in mol per litre per second. For order one, purely per second. For order two, litre per mole per second. Even a fractional order like three halves gives half-power units.
So here is a free self-check. If you compute an order but your k comes out with the wrong units for that order, one of them is wrong. Reconcile before moving on.
अब rate constant, k, को pin down करते हैं, जिसे specific reaction rate भी कहते हैं। ये rate की वो value है जब हर reactant concentration एक के बराबर हो।
Definition rate equals k times concentration terms से आती है: सभी concentrations को unity कर दो, तो rate बस k रह जाता है।
इसकी तीन defining properties याद रखिए। k concentration पर depend नहीं करता, temperature पर depend करता है, और बड़ा k मतलब faster reaction।

अब वो diagnostic जो याद रखने लायक है। चूँकि k equals rate divided by concentration to the power n, इसकी units हैं mol per litre, whole raised to one minus n, times per second. जो tidy होकर बनता है mol to the one minus n, litre to the n minus one, per second।
ये table बस हर order को उस formula में डालती है। ध्यान दीजिए units सच में order के साथ बदलती हैं, यही उन्हें useful बनाता है।

Order zero के लिए k, mol per litre per second में है। Order one के लिए सिर्फ़ per second। Order two के लिए litre per mole per second। यहाँ तक कि three halves जैसा fractional order half-power units देता है।
तो यहाँ एक free self-check है। अगर आपका order और k की units match न करें, तो दोनों में से एक गलत है। आगे बढ़ने से पहले reconcile कीजिए।

sections.title: Order, Units of k, and Rate Scaling (CBSE)

board_events.text: CBSE: for $2A + B \rightarrow C$, Rate $= k[A][B]^2$

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="260" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="28" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Rate = k[A][B]² — double [A], triple [B]</text><text x="60" y="80" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="13">[A] ×2 → factor 2¹ = 2</text><text x="60" y="110" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="13">[B] ×3 → factor 3² = 9</text><line x1="55" y1="130" x2="405" y2="130" stroke="#8c959f" stroke-width="1"/><text x="60" y="165" fill="#111111" font-size="14">combined: 2 × 9</text><rect x="230" y="145" width="175" height="40" rx="8" fill="#fff8c5" stroke="#9a6700"/><text x="317" y="172" fill="#d1242f" font-size="18" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">= 18×</text><text x="230" y="225" fill="#9a6700" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">the "2" in 2A never enters an experimental rate law</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Doubling [A] and tripling [B] multiplies the rate by 2 times 9 = 18

board_events.text: (i) Order in $A$ is 1, order in $B$ is 2, so overall order is 3.
(iii) Double $[A]$, triple $[B]$: new rate $= k(2[A])(3[B])^2$.
We never touched the coefficient '2' in $2A$ — coefficients never enter an experimental rate law.

segments.text: First worked example, C B S E board level. For the reaction two A plus B gives C, the experimentally given rate law is rate equals k times A times B squared.
The visual previews the punchline. Doubling A brings a factor of two, tripling B brings a factor of nine, and together they multiply the rate by eighteen.
Part one, the orders. The exponent of A is one, so it is first order in A. The exponent of B is two, so second order in B. The overall order is one plus two, which is three.

Part two, the units of k. Using mol to the one minus n, litre to the n minus one, per second with n equal to three, we get mol to the minus two, litre squared, per second, which we write as litre squared per mole squared per second.
Part three, the scaling. Replace A by two A and B by three B. The new rate is k times two A times the quantity three B, squared.
Pull the numbers out. Two, times three squared which is nine, gives two times nine, so eighteen times the old rate. The rate becomes eighteen times the original.
And notice what we did not do. We never touched the coefficient two sitting in front of A in the equation. Stoichiometric coefficients never enter an experimentally given rate law.
पहला worked example, C B S E board level. Reaction two A plus B gives C के लिए, experimentally दिया गया rate law है rate equals k times A times B squared।
Visual punchline पहले ही दिखा देता है। A को double करने पर factor दो, B को triple करने पर factor नौ, और मिलकर rate को अठारह गुना कर देते हैं।
Part one, orders. A का exponent one है, तो A में first order. B का exponent two है, तो B में second order. Overall order one plus two, यानी तीन।

Part two, k की units. mol to the one minus n, litre to the n minus one, per second में n बराबर तीन डालने पर मिलता है mol to the minus two, litre squared, per second, जिसे हम litre squared per mole squared per second लिखते हैं।
Part three, scaling. A को two A से और B को three B से replace करो। नया rate है k times two A times the quantity three B, squared।
Numbers बाहर निकालो। दो, times three squared जो नौ है, देता है दो times नौ, यानी अठारह गुना पुराना rate। Rate अठारह गुना हो जाता है।
और ध्यान दीजिए हमने क्या नहीं किया। हमने equation में A के आगे बैठे coefficient two को छुआ तक नहीं। Stoichiometric coefficients कभी experimental rate law में नहीं घुसते।

board_events.text: Experiments 1 to 2: $[P]$ doubles, $[Q]$ fixed, rate doubles.
Experiments 1 to 3: $[Q]$ triples, $[P]$ fixed, rate rises ninefold.
Overall order $= 1 + 2 = 3$. The ratio is your friend; the absolute numbers are noise.
Trap: computing $k$ for every row wastes time, and assuming order $= 1+1$ from '1 P, 1 Q' is wrong.

segments.text: Second example, a N E E T speed trap. You are handed a table of initial-rate data for P plus Q gives R, and you must find the overall order fast.
Here is the table. The whole trick is to compare only the rows where a single concentration changed, so the rate change can be pinned on that one reactant.
Compare experiments one and two. P doubles, Q stays fixed, and the rate doubles.
So two equals two to the power x, which means x is one. The reaction is first order in P.
Now experiments one and three. Q triples, P stays fixed, and the rate jumps ninefold, from two times ten to the minus three up to one point eight times ten to the minus two.
That gives nine equals three to the power y, so y is two. Second order in Q.
Overall order is one plus two, which is three. The ratio is your friend here, and the absolute numbers are just noise.

Beware the trap. The panicked student computes k for every row, wasting ninety seconds, or worse, assumes the order is one plus one from the one P, one Q stoichiometry. Always pick the two rows where only one concentration moved.
दूसरा example, एक N E E T speed trap. आपको P plus Q gives R के लिए initial-rate data की table दी जाती है, और overall order जल्दी निकालना है।
ये रही table। पूरा trick है सिर्फ़ उन rows को compare करना जहाँ एक ही concentration बदली हो, ताकि rate change उसी एक reactant पर pin हो सके।
Experiments one और two compare करो। P double होता है, Q fixed रहता है, और rate double हो जाता है।
तो two equals two to the power x, यानी x एक है। Reaction P में first order है।
अब experiments one और three। Q triple होता है, P fixed रहता है, और rate नौ गुना बढ़ता है, two into ten to the minus three से one point eight into ten to the minus two तक।
इससे मिलता है nine equals three to the power y, तो y दो है। Q में second order।
Overall order one plus two, यानी तीन। यहाँ ratio आपका दोस्त है, और absolute numbers बस noise।

<excited> Trap से बचिए। घबराया हुआ student हर row के लिए k compute करता है, नब्बे seconds बर्बाद करता है, या इससे भी बुरा, one P one Q stoichiometry से order one plus one मान लेता है। हमेशा वो दो rows चुनो जहाँ सिर्फ़ एक concentration बदली हो।

sections.title: Stoichiometric Rate Relations in Ammonia Oxidation (JEE Main)

board_events.text: JEE Main: $4NH_3 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 4NO + 6H_2O$

board_events.caption: One reaction rate links every species through its coefficient

board_events.text: Given $d[NO]/dt = 3.6\times10^{-3}$, the single reaction rate is a quarter of that.
Disappearance of $O_2$ is five times the rate; of $NH_3$, four times.
Sensibly, $NH_3$ disappears as fast as $NO$ forms — equal coefficients.

segments.text: Third example, J E E Main level, tying stoichiometric rate relations to a rate law. The reaction is the catalytic oxidation of ammonia, four N H three plus five O two giving four N O plus six H two O.
The diagram is the key: one single reaction rate is linked to every species through its coefficient. Read it top to bottom.
In symbols, rate equals minus one quarter d N H three by d t, equals minus one fifth d O two by d t, equals plus one quarter d N O by d t, equals plus one sixth d H two O by d t.
We are told the rate of formation of N O is three point six times ten to the minus three. The single reaction rate is one quarter of that, because N O carries a coefficient of four.
So the rate of reaction is one quarter of three point six times ten to the minus three, which is nine point zero times ten to the minus four mol per litre per second.

Now scale back up for the others. Oxygen disappears at five times the reaction rate, giving four point five times ten to the minus three. Ammonia disappears at four times the rate, giving three point six times ten to the minus three.
That last number is a nice sanity check. Ammonia disappears exactly as fast as N O forms, because both carry the coefficient four.
Finally the rate law. First order in ammonia and first order in oxygen gives rate equals k times ammonia times oxygen, overall order two, so k is in litre per mole per second.

तीसरा example, J E E Main level, जो stoichiometric rate relations को rate law से जोड़ता है। Reaction है ammonia का catalytic oxidation, four N H three plus five O two giving four N O plus six H two O।
Diagram key है: एक single reaction rate हर species से उसके coefficient के ज़रिए जुड़ा है। ऊपर से नीचे पढ़िए।
Symbols में, rate equals minus one quarter d N H three by d t, equals minus one fifth d O two by d t, equals plus one quarter d N O by d t, equals plus one sixth d H two O by d t।
हमें बताया गया है N O के बनने का rate three point six into ten to the minus three है। Single reaction rate उसका एक चौथाई है, क्योंकि N O का coefficient चार है।
तो reaction का rate three point six into ten to the minus three का एक चौथाई है, यानी nine point zero into ten to the minus four mol per litre per second।

अब बाकियों के लिए वापस scale करो। Oxygen reaction rate के पाँच गुना rate पर गायब होता है, यानी four point five into ten to the minus three. Ammonia चार गुना rate पर, यानी three point six into ten to the minus three।
वो आख़िरी number एक अच्छा sanity check है। Ammonia बिलकुल उतनी ही तेज़ी से गायब होता है जितनी तेज़ी से N O बनता है, क्योंकि दोनों का coefficient चार है।
आख़िर में rate law. Ammonia में first order और oxygen में first order देता है rate equals k times ammonia times oxygen, overall order दो, तो k litre per mole per second में है।

board_events.caption: Fast pre-equilibrium feeds an intermediate into the slow step; substitute it out

board_events.text: Slow step is rate-determining, so Rate $= k_2[A_2][B]$.
But $A_2$ is an intermediate — eliminate it using the fast equilibrium.
Overall order $= 2 + 1 = 3$, but the slow step is only bimolecular (molecularity 2).
Order exceeds the slow step's molecularity because the slow step swallowed an intermediate.

segments.text: Fourth example, J E E Advanced, and the discriminating one. A reaction with overall stoichiometry two A plus B giving A two B is proposed to run through two steps.
The scheme is on the board. Step one is a fast equilibrium in which two A combine to form the intermediate A two. Step two, the slow one, is A two plus B giving the product.
Since the slow step is rate-determining, we start by writing the rate as k two times A two times B, using the slow step's own species.
But A two is a reactive intermediate. Its concentration is not something we control, so we cannot leave it in the answer. We must eliminate it.

Step one is a fast equilibrium, so its forward and reverse rates are essentially balanced. That gives k one A squared equals k minus one times A two, so A two equals k one over k minus one, times A squared.
Substitute that in. The rate becomes k two times k one over k minus one, times A squared, times B, which we bundle as an observed constant times A squared times B.
So the overall order is two plus one, which is three. Yet the slow step, A two plus B, involves only two species, so its molecularity is two, bimolecular.

That is the whole point. The overall order, three, exceeds the slow step's molecularity, two, precisely because the slow step swallowed an intermediate that carried an extra factor of A in through the pre-equilibrium.
चौथा example, J E E Advanced, और सबसे discriminating वाला। Overall stoichiometry two A plus B giving A two B वाली reaction दो steps से proceed करने का proposal है।
Scheme board पर है। Step one एक fast equilibrium है जिसमें दो A मिलकर intermediate A two बनाते हैं। Step two, slow वाला, है A two plus B giving product।
चूँकि slow step rate-determining है, हम rate को k two times A two times B के रूप में लिखकर शुरू करते हैं, slow step की अपनी species use करके।
पर A two एक reactive intermediate है। इसकी concentration हमारे control में नहीं, तो हम इसे answer में नहीं छोड़ सकते। इसे eliminate करना होगा।

Step one एक fast equilibrium है, तो इसके forward और reverse rates essentially balanced हैं। इससे k one A squared equals k minus one times A two, यानी A two equals k one over k minus one, times A squared।
इसे substitute करो। Rate बनता है k two times k one over k minus one, times A squared, times B, जिसे हम observed constant times A squared times B के रूप में bundle करते हैं।
तो overall order two plus one, यानी तीन। फिर भी slow step, A two plus B, में सिर्फ़ दो species हैं, तो उसकी molecularity दो है, bimolecular।
<whisper> यही पूरी बात है। Overall order तीन, slow step की molecularity दो से ज़्यादा है, ठीक इसलिए क्योंकि slow step ने एक intermediate निगल लिया जो pre-equilibrium से A का एक extra factor साथ लाया।

sections.title: Common Pitfalls: Order, Molecularity and the Coefficient Trap

board_events.text: Where marks quietly leak away
Reading order off the balanced equation — the most expensive mistake in the chapter.
The equation gives stoichiometry, not kinetics. Only experiment (or an 'elementary' label) gives the rate law.
Confusing order with molecularity: order may be 0, fractional, negative; molecularity is a counted 1, 2 or 3.
If you ever write 'molecularity = 1.5' or 'molecularity of the overall complex reaction', stop.
Dropping the coefficient factor, wrongly equating the rates of $N_2$, $H_2$ and $NH_3$.
In a mechanism, always substitute out intermediates before reading off the order.
Pro-tip: treat the units of $k$ as a free check on your order — a mismatch means one is wrong.

segments.text: Let us close subtopic one with the pitfalls that quietly drain marks, and the pro-tips that save them.
The most expensive mistake in the whole chapter: reading the order straight off the balanced equation. Resist it every single time.
The equation tells you stoichiometry, how atoms balance, not kinetics, how fast things go. Only experiment, or an explicit elementary label, gives you the true rate law.
Second, confusing order with molecularity. Order is experimental and can be zero, a fraction, or negative. Molecularity is a counted whole number, one, two, or three.
So if you ever find yourself writing molecularity equals one point five, or talking about the molecularity of an overall complex reaction, stop. Neither exists.
Third, dropping the coefficient factor when you write the single rate of reaction, and then wrongly equating the rates of nitrogen, hydrogen, and ammonia. Always divide each by its coefficient.
And in any mechanism problem, always substitute out the intermediate before reading off the order. Leaving an undetermined intermediate in the final rate law gives the wrong order.

<whisper> One pro-tip to carry with you: the units of k are a free verification of your order. If you computed order two but k came out in per second, one of them is wrong. Reconcile before you move on.
Subtopic one को उन pitfalls के साथ बंद करते हैं जो चुपचाप marks उड़ाते हैं, और उन pro-tips के साथ जो उन्हें बचाते हैं।
पूरे chapter की सबसे महँगी गलती: order को सीधे balanced equation से पढ़ना। हर बार इसका विरोध कीजिए।
Equation आपको stoichiometry बताती है, यानी atoms कैसे balance होते हैं, kinetics नहीं, यानी चीज़ें कितनी तेज़ चलती हैं। सिर्फ़ experiment, या explicit elementary label, असली rate law देता है।
दूसरा, order को molecularity से confuse करना। Order experimental है और zero, fraction, या negative हो सकता है। Molecularity एक counted whole number है — एक, दो या तीन।
तो अगर आप कभी molecularity equals one point five लिखने लगें, या किसी overall complex reaction की molecularity की बात करें, तो रुक जाइए। इनमें से कुछ भी exist नहीं करता।
तीसरा, single rate of reaction लिखते समय coefficient factor छोड़ देना, और फिर nitrogen, hydrogen, ammonia के rates को गलती से बराबर मान लेना। हमेशा हर एक को उसके coefficient से divide करो।
और किसी भी mechanism problem में, order पढ़ने से पहले हमेशा intermediate को substitute करो। Final rate law में एक undetermined intermediate छोड़ने से गलत order आता है।
<whisper> साथ ले जाने वाली एक pro-tip: k की units आपके order का free verification हैं। अगर आपने order two निकाला पर k per second में आया, तो एक गलत है। आगे बढ़ने से पहले reconcile कीजिए।

sections.title: Why Integrate? From Differential to Integrated Rate Laws

board_events.text: From 'rate right now' to 'concentration at time $t$'

board_events.caption: Integrating the differential law once gives a direct concentration-versus-time relationship

board_events.text: The differential rate law needs the slope of a tangent at every instant — hard to measure.
Integrated rate equations do the calculus once, ahead of time.
The result is a clean relationship between concentration and clock time — both directly readable.
Different decay behaviours give different shapes, which is how order is identified.
Picture a matka with a small hole: not 'how fast now' but 'what level after ten minutes'.

segments.text: In the last subtopic we wrote the differential rate law, rate as a function of concentration at an instant. Beautiful for theory, but painful in the lab.

This picture captures the whole idea. On the left, the differential law needs the slope of a tangent at every moment, which is hard to measure accurately. The integral sign takes us to the right, where concentration versus clock time is directly readable.
Why is the differential form painful? Because to use it you would need the tangent slope of a curve at every single moment. That is fiddly and error-prone.
Integrated rate equations solve this elegantly. We do the calculus once, ahead of time, and then reuse the result forever.
What we are left with is a clean relationship between concentration and clock time, two things you can read straight off an experiment without any tangent-drawing.
And there is a bonus. Different leak behaviours give different shapes, and that is precisely what lets us tell a zero-order reaction from a first-order one.

Think of tracking the water level in a matka, a clay pot with a small hole. The differential law says how fast the level drops right now. What you really want is a formula for the level after ten minutes. Integrating gives exactly that.
पिछले subtopic में हमने differential rate law लिखा था, rate as a function of concentration at an instant. Theory के लिए बढ़िया, पर lab में painful।

ये picture पूरा idea पकड़ती है। बाईं तरफ़, differential law को हर moment tangent का slope चाहिए, जो accurately measure करना मुश्किल है। Integral sign हमें दाईं तरफ़ ले जाता है, जहाँ concentration versus clock time सीधे readable है।
Differential form painful क्यों है? क्योंकि इसे use करने के लिए आपको हर एक moment पर curve की tangent slope चाहिए। वो fiddly और error-prone है।
Integrated rate equations इसे elegantly solve करते हैं। हम calculus एक बार, पहले ही कर लेते हैं, और फिर result को हमेशा के लिए reuse करते हैं।
हमारे पास बचता है concentration और clock time के बीच एक clean relationship, दो चीज़ें जो आप experiment से सीधे पढ़ सकते हैं, बिना कोई tangent खींचे।
और एक bonus भी है। अलग-अलग leak behaviours अलग shapes देते हैं, और यही हमें zero-order reaction को first-order से बताने देता है।

एक matka सोचिए, एक मिट्टी का बर्तन जिसमें छोटा सा छेद है। Differential law बताता है अभी level कितनी तेज़ी से गिर रहा है। पर आप सच में चाहते हैं दस minute बाद का level। Integrate करने पर बिलकुल वही मिलता है।

sections.title: Zero Order vs First Order: Two Decay Shapes

board_events.text: Two very different decay curves

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="260" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="40" y1="30" x2="40" y2="200" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="40" y1="200" x2="210" y2="200" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="55" y1="45" x2="190" y2="195" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="3"/><text x="125" y="225" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">time</text><text x="120" y="20" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">ZERO order</text><text x="130" y="120" fill="#111111" font-size="11">straight line</text><text x="130" y="136" fill="#111111" font-size="11">(tap, fixed flow)</text><line x1="260" y1="30" x2="260" y2="200" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="260" y1="200" x2="430" y2="200" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M270,45 C300,120 340,175 425,193" fill="none" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="3"/><text x="345" y="225" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">time</text><text x="345" y="20" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">FIRST order</text><text x="350" y="90" fill="#111111" font-size="11">exponential</text><text x="350" y="106" fill="#111111" font-size="11">decay</text><text x="230" y="250" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">y-axis: [R]</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Zero order: straight-line fall. First order: exponential decay.

board_events.text: Zero order: concentration falls in a perfectly straight line — like a tap at fixed flow.
First order: the more reactant present, the faster it goes — a smooth exponential curve.
Why would a reaction ignore concentration? Some other resource sets the pace.
Classic cases: a surface-catalysed decomposition with a saturated catalyst, or a light-limited photochemical step.
When that resource stops being limiting, the zero-order description breaks down.

segments.text: Now let us picture the two decay shapes side by side, because the shapes themselves reveal the order.
On the left, a zero-order reaction: the concentration falls along a perfectly straight line. On the right, a first-order reaction: a smooth exponential curve that bends and never quite reaches zero.
A zero-order reaction is like a tap running at a fixed flow regardless of how full the tank is. The concentration drops in a straight line with time, the same amount every second.
A first-order reaction is different. The more reactant present, the faster it goes, so the concentration falls along a smooth exponential curve that flattens as it approaches zero.
<curious> But why would any reaction ignore concentration and behave as zero order? Usually because some other resource, not the bulk reactant, sets the pace.

Two classic cases. A surface-catalysed decomposition where the catalyst surface is fully saturated, so adding more gas cannot speed anything up. And a photochemical step limited by a fixed light intensity.

The key caveat: the moment that limiting resource stops being the bottleneck, when the surface frees up or the reactant runs low, the zero-order description breaks down. That is why zero-order kinetics usually holds only over a finite window.
अब दोनों decay shapes को साथ-साथ देखते हैं, क्योंकि shapes खुद order बता देते हैं।

बाईं तरफ़, एक zero-order reaction: concentration एक perfectly straight line में गिरती है। दाईं तरफ़, एक first-order reaction: एक smooth exponential curve जो झुकती है और कभी बिलकुल zero तक नहीं पहुँचती।
Zero-order reaction एक ऐसे नल जैसी है जो fixed flow पर चलता है, चाहे tank कितना भी भरा हो। Concentration time के साथ straight line में गिरती है, हर second वही amount।
First-order reaction अलग है। जितना ज़्यादा reactant मौजूद, उतनी तेज़ चलती है, तो concentration एक smooth exponential curve में गिरती है जो zero के पास flatten हो जाती है।
<curious> पर कोई reaction concentration को ignore करके zero order क्यों behave करेगी? आमतौर पर क्योंकि कोई और resource, bulk reactant नहीं, pace set करता है।

दो classic cases. एक surface-catalysed decomposition जहाँ catalyst surface पूरी तरह saturated है, तो ज़्यादा gas डालने से कुछ तेज़ नहीं होता। और एक photochemical step जो fixed light intensity से limited है।

Key caveat: जिस पल वो limiting resource bottleneck होना बंद करता है, जब surface खाली होता है या reactant कम पड़ता है, zero-order description टूट जाती है। इसीलिए zero-order kinetics आमतौर पर सिर्फ़ एक finite window में ही टिकती है।

sections.title: How Half-Life Fingerprints the Order

board_events.text: The half-life $t_{1/2}$ and what it reveals

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="250" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="26" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">How t½ tracks the starting amount</text><rect x="30" y="45" width="190" height="170" rx="10" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="125" y="72" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">FIRST order</text><text x="125" y="100" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">t½ independent</text><text x="125" y="118" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">of [R]₀</text><text x="125" y="150" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">every halving</text><text x="125" y="168" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">takes equal time</text><text x="125" y="198" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">t½ = 0.693/k</text><rect x="240" y="45" width="190" height="170" rx="10" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="2"/><text x="335" y="72" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">ZERO order</text><text x="335" y="100" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">t½ ∝ [R]₀</text><text x="335" y="128" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">start with more</text><text x="335" y="146" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">→ first halving</text><text x="335" y="164" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">takes longer</text><text x="335" y="198" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">t½ = [R]₀/2k</text></svg>
board_events.caption: First-order half-life is independent of starting amount; zero-order half-life scales with it

board_events.text: $t_{1/2}$ is the time for the concentration to fall to half its starting value.
First order: $t_{1/2}$ is completely independent of the initial concentration.
So '75% done in two half-lives, 87.5% in three' works as a mental shortcut.
Zero order: $t_{1/2}$ is directly proportional to the initial concentration.
So you can identify the order just by watching how the half-life behaves — no rate-law table needed.

segments.text: That last point leads to the chapter's most famous quantity, the half-life, written t one half.
The picture says it all. For a first-order reaction, every halving takes the same time no matter where you start. For zero order, the half-life stretches in proportion to how much you start with.
First the definition. The half-life is simply the time for the concentration to fall to half of its starting value.

Now the deep insight examiners love. For a first-order reaction, the half-life is completely independent of the initial concentration. Whether you start with a bucket or a drop, every halving takes the same time.
That independence is why the mental shortcut works: seventy five percent done in two half-lives, eighty seven point five percent in three, because each half-life removes half of what remains.
For a zero-order reaction, it is the opposite. The half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration. Start with more, and the first halving takes proportionally longer.
This single contrast is powerful. You can identify the order just by watching how the half-life behaves as you change the starting concentration, with no rate-law table at all.
वो आख़िरी point chapter की सबसे famous quantity तक ले जाता है, half-life, जिसे हम t one half लिखते हैं।
Picture सब कुछ कह देती है। First-order reaction के लिए, हर halving एक ही time लेती है चाहे आप कहीं से भी शुरू करें। Zero order के लिए, half-life उतनी ही खिंचती है जितना आप शुरू में लेते हैं।
पहले definition। Half-life बस वो time है जिसमें concentration अपनी starting value की आधी हो जाती है।

अब वो deep insight जो examiners को बहुत पसंद है। First-order reaction के लिए, half-life initial concentration से पूरी तरह independent है। चाहे आप एक बाल्टी से शुरू करें या एक बूँद से, हर halving एक ही time लेती है।
यही independence shortcut को काम करने देती है: seventy five percent done in two half-lives, eighty seven point five percent in three, क्योंकि हर half-life बचे हुए का आधा हटाती है।
Zero-order reaction के लिए उल्टा है। Half-life initial concentration के directly proportional है। ज़्यादा से शुरू करो, और पहली halving proportionally ज़्यादा time लेती है।
ये single contrast powerful है। आप order को सिर्फ़ ये देखकर पहचान सकते हैं कि starting concentration बदलने पर half-life कैसे behave करता है, बिना किसी rate-law table के।

sections.title: Derivation: The Zero-Order Integrated Rate Equation

board_events.text: Integrating the zero-order rate law

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="260" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="60" y1="30" x2="60" y2="210" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="210" x2="420" y2="210" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><text x="30" y="120" fill="#111111" font-size="13" transform="rotate(-90 30 120)">[R]</text><text x="240" y="245" fill="#111111" font-size="13">time / s</text><circle cx="60" cy="50" r="4" fill="#1f6feb"/><text x="70" y="48" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="12">[R]₀  (intercept)</text><line x1="60" y1="50" x2="360" y2="210" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="3"/><text x="230" y="130" fill="#d1242f" font-size="13">slope = −k</text><text x="150" y="200" fill="#111111" font-size="12">[R] = [R]₀ − kt</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Zero order gives a straight line of [R] against t with slope minus k

board_events.text: Separate and integrate both sides.
At $t=0$, $[R]=[R]_0$, so the constant $I = [R]_0$.

segments.text: Let us actually derive the zero-order integrated equation, a standard board question.
Here is the target shape. Plotting concentration of R against time gives a straight descending line whose slope is minus k and whose intercept is the starting concentration.
A zero-order rate means the rate is independent of concentration. So minus d R by d t equals k times R to the power zero, which is just k. The reaction proceeds at a fixed pace set only by k.
Now separate the variables and integrate both sides. The concentration change on one side, time on the other.
Integrating gives R equals minus k t plus an integration constant, which I will call capital I.
We fix that constant with the initial condition. At time zero, the concentration is R naught, so capital I equals R naught.
That gives the clean result: concentration of R equals R naught minus k t. This is the equation of a straight line, y equals m x plus c, with slope minus k.

For the half-life, set the concentration to half of R naught. Half R naught equals R naught minus k times t one half, which rearranges to t one half equals R naught over two k, showing the half-life is proportional to the starting concentration.
चलिए zero-order integrated equation को actually derive करते हैं, एक standard board question।
ये रहा target shape। Concentration of R को time के against plot करने पर एक straight descending line मिलती है जिसका slope minus k है और intercept starting concentration।
Zero-order rate मतलब rate concentration से independent है। तो minus d R by d t equals k times R to the power zero, जो बस k है। Reaction एक fixed pace पर चलती है जो सिर्फ़ k से set होती है।
अब variables separate करके दोनों sides integrate करो। एक तरफ़ concentration change, दूसरी तरफ़ time।
Integrate करने पर मिलता है R equals minus k t plus an integration constant, जिसे मैं capital I कहूँगा।
उस constant को initial condition से fix करते हैं। Time zero पर concentration R naught है, तो capital I equals R naught।
इससे clean result मिलता है: concentration of R equals R naught minus k t. ये एक straight line का equation है, y equals m x plus c, slope minus k के साथ।

Half-life के लिए, concentration को R naught की आधी set करो। Half R naught equals R naught minus k times t one half, जो rearrange होकर देता है t one half equals R naught over two k, दिखाता है कि half-life starting concentration के proportional है।

sections.title: Derivation: The First-Order Integrated Rate Equation

board_events.text: Integrating the first-order rate law

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="260" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="60" y1="30" x2="60" y2="210" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="210" x2="420" y2="210" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><text x="24" y="140" fill="#111111" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 24 140)">log([R]₀/[R])</text><text x="240" y="245" fill="#111111" font-size="13">time / s</text><line x1="60" y1="210" x2="380" y2="55" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="60" cy="210" r="4" fill="#1a7f37"/><text x="70" y="200" fill="#111111" font-size="12">through the origin</text><text x="250" y="110" fill="#d1242f" font-size="13">slope = k / 2.303</text></svg>
board_events.caption: A plot of log([R]0/[R]) against t is a straight line through the origin

board_events.text: Separating variables isolates concentration on one side, time on the other.
Half-life: $t_{1/2} = 0.693/k$ — the $[R]_0$ cancels, so it is independent of the start.

segments.text: Now the first-order integrated equation, the workhorse of the whole chapter.
Its diagnostic plot is on the board: log of R naught over R, against time, is a straight line passing through the origin with slope k over two point three zero three.
Start from the rate law. Minus d R by d t equals k times R. Divide through so that d R over R sits on the left, giving d R over R equals minus k d t.
The point of separating variables is to isolate concentration on one side and time on the other, so each can be integrated independently.
Integrating gives natural log of R equals minus k t plus natural log of R naught, where the constant is natural log of R naught from time zero.
Rearranged into exam form: natural log of R naught over R equals k t. In base-ten logs that is k equals two point three zero three over t, times log of R naught over R.
Taking the antilog gives the exponential decay form, R equals R naught times e to the minus k t. The familiar smooth curve.

For the half-life, set R to half of R naught. The R naught cancels, and you are left with t one half equals zero point six nine three over k, which proves the first-order half-life is independent of how much you start with.
अब first-order integrated equation, पूरे chapter का workhorse।
इसका diagnostic plot board पर है: log of R naught over R, time के against, एक straight line है जो origin से गुज़रती है और जिसका slope k over two point three zero three है।
Rate law से शुरू करो। Minus d R by d t equals k times R. दोनों तरफ़ divide करो ताकि d R over R बाईं तरफ़ बैठे, यानी d R over R equals minus k d t।
Variables separate करने का मक़सद है concentration को एक तरफ़ और time को दूसरी तरफ़ isolate करना, ताकि हर एक independently integrate हो सके।
Integrate करने पर मिलता है natural log of R equals minus k t plus natural log of R naught, जहाँ constant time zero से natural log of R naught है।
Exam form में rearrange: natural log of R naught over R equals k t. Base-ten logs में वो k equals two point three zero three over t, times log of R naught over R।
Antilog लेने पर exponential decay form मिलता है, R equals R naught times e to the minus k t. वही जाना-पहचाना smooth curve।

Half-life के लिए, R को R naught की आधी set करो। R naught cancel हो जाता है, और बचता है t one half equals zero point six nine three over k, जो साबित करता है कि first-order half-life starting amount से independent है।

sections.title: Derivation: First-Order Kinetics from Total Pressure

board_events.text: Tracking a gas reaction by pressure

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 182" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="182" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="34" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">pᵗ = pᵢ + x  ⇒  pᵑ = 2pᵢ − pᵗ</text><rect x="20" y="60" width="440" height="34" fill="#1f6feb"/><text x="110" y="82" fill="#ffffff" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">A(g)</text><text x="265" y="82" fill="#ffffff" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">→ B(g)</text><text x="395" y="82" fill="#ffffff" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">+ C(g)</text><rect x="20" y="94" width="440" height="34" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#d0d7de"/><text x="110" y="116" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">t = 0:  pᵢ</text><text x="265" y="116" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">0</text><text x="395" y="116" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">0</text><rect x="20" y="128" width="440" height="34" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#d0d7de"/><text x="110" y="150" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">t:  pᵢ − x</text><text x="265" y="150" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">x</text><text x="395" y="150" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">x</text><rect x="20" y="60" width="440" height="102" fill="none" stroke="#8c959f" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg>
board_events.caption: Pressure bookkeeping for A(g) to B(g) + C(g); recover p_A from total pressure

board_events.text: For $A(g) \rightarrow B(g) + C(g)$ from pure $A$ at $p_i$, let $x$ be the fall in $A$'s pressure.
Each of $B$ and $C$ rises by $x$, so the total pressure is $p_t = p_i + x$.

board_events.latex: x = p_t - p_i \implies p_A = p_i - x = 2p_i - p_t

board_events.text: The manometer reads $p_t$, but the rate law needs $p_A$ — recover it from the balance.

segments.text: For gas-phase reactions we rarely measure concentration directly. We measure total pressure with a manometer, so we need to convert.
This little table does the bookkeeping. Consider A gas going to B gas plus C gas, starting from pure A at initial pressure p i. Let x be the fall in A's pressure at time t.

At fixed temperature and volume, each species' partial pressure is proportional to its moles, so we can track the reaction in pressure units exactly as in concentration units. Let x be how much A's pressure has dropped.
By stoichiometry, B and C each rise by x. So the surviving pressure of A is p i minus x, while B and C are each x.
Add them up. The total pressure is p i minus x, plus x, plus x, which is p i plus x. So x equals p t minus p i, and the surviving pressure of A is two p i minus p t.
Substitute that into the first-order law written in pressure, and you get the working equation: k equals two point three zero three over t, times log of p i over the quantity two p i minus p t.
The single trap to remember: the manometer reads the total pressure, but the rate law needs the reactant's own partial pressure, which you recover from the stoichiometric balance.
Gas-phase reactions के लिए हम शायद ही कभी concentration सीधे measure करते हैं। हम manometer से total pressure measure करते हैं, तो convert करना पड़ता है।
ये छोटी table वही bookkeeping करती है। सोचिए A gas going to B gas plus C gas, pure A से initial pressure p i पर शुरू। Let x be A के pressure में गिरावट at time t।

Fixed temperature और volume पर, हर species का partial pressure उसके moles के proportional है, तो हम reaction को pressure units में exactly वैसे ही track कर सकते हैं जैसे concentration units में। Let x be A का pressure कितना गिरा।
Stoichiometry से, B और C हर एक x से बढ़ते हैं। तो A का surviving pressure p i minus x है, जबकि B और C हर एक x।
जोड़ लो। Total pressure है p i minus x, plus x, plus x, यानी p i plus x. तो x equals p t minus p i, और A का surviving pressure two p i minus p t।
इसे pressure में लिखे first-order law में substitute करो, और आपको working equation मिलता है: k equals two point three zero three over t, times log of p i over the quantity two p i minus p t।
याद रखने वाला single trap: manometer total pressure पढ़ता है, पर rate law को reactant का अपना partial pressure चाहिए, जिसे आप stoichiometric balance से recover करते हैं।

board_events.text: Your consolidated toolkit for this subtopic

board_events.text: Zero order plots $[R]$ vs $t$ (slope $-k$); first order plots $\log([R]_0/[R])$ vs $t$ (slope $k/2.303$).
Full pattern: zero order $t_{1/2}\propto[R]_0$; first ignores it; second $t_{1/2}\propto 1/[R]_0$.
Consistency check: $t_{3/4}/t_{1/2} = 2^{\,n-1}+1$ — gives 2 for first order, 3 for second.

segments.text: Let us consolidate the toolkit for this subtopic in one place, so any section can jump straight to it.
Zero order: concentration equals R naught minus k t, and the half-life is R naught over two k, which is proportional to the starting concentration.
First order: k equals two point three zero three over t, times log of R naught over R, and the half-life is zero point six nine three over k, independent of the start.
These two plots are the fingerprints. Zero order gives a straight line of concentration against time. First order gives a straight line of log R naught over R against time.
So for zero order you plot concentration against time and read a slope of minus k. For first order you plot log of R naught over R against time and read a slope of k over two point three zero three.

There is also a master relationship for reading order from half-life data. Log of the half-life equals one minus n, times log of the starting concentration, plus a constant. So a plot of log half-life against log starting concentration has slope one minus n.
The full pattern is worth memorising. Zero order half-life scales with the starting concentration, first order ignores it, and second order scales with one over the starting concentration.

And a handy consistency check: the ratio of the three-quarter life to the half-life equals two to the n minus one, plus one. That gives two for first order and three for second order, a fast check on any completion answer.
चलिए इस subtopic का toolkit एक जगह consolidate करते हैं, ताकि कोई भी section सीधे यहाँ jump कर सके।
Zero order: concentration equals R naught minus k t, और half-life R naught over two k है, जो starting concentration के proportional है।
First order: k equals two point three zero three over t, times log of R naught over R, और half-life zero point six nine three over k है, start से independent।
ये दो plots fingerprints हैं। Zero order concentration को time के against straight line देता है। First order log R naught over R को time के against straight line देता है।

तो zero order के लिए concentration को time के against plot करो और slope minus k पढ़ो। First order के लिए log of R naught over R को time के against plot करो और slope k over two point three zero three पढ़ो।

Half-life data से order पढ़ने का एक master relationship भी है। Log of half-life equals one minus n, times log of starting concentration, plus a constant. तो log half-life vs log starting concentration का slope one minus n है।
पूरा pattern याद रखने लायक है। Zero order half-life starting concentration के साथ scale करता है, first order उसे ignore करता है, और second order one over starting concentration के साथ scale करता है।

और एक handy consistency check: three-quarter life और half-life का ratio equals two to the n minus one, plus one. जो first order के लिए दो और second order के लिए तीन देता है, किसी भी completion answer का fast check।

sections.title: Half-Life and Time for 75% Completion (CBSE)

board_events.text: CBSE: first order, $k = 2.31\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$
(a) The half-life is $0.693/k$.
(b) After 75% consumed, a quarter remains — that is two successive halvings.

board_events.text: Check: $t = \frac{2.303}{k}\log 4 \approx 600$ s — the formula agrees.

segments.text: First worked example of subtopic two, C B S E board level. A first-order reaction has rate constant k equal to two point three one times ten to the minus three per second.
Part a asks for the half-life. For first order the half-life is simply zero point six nine three over k.
Plug in. Zero point six nine three divided by two point three one times ten to the minus three gives three hundred seconds. A clean half-life.
Part b asks for the time for seventy five percent to be consumed. After seventy five percent is gone, a quarter of the reactant remains, and a quarter is two successive halvings.
So the time is two half-lives, two times three hundred, which is six hundred seconds. No integration needed.
This ladder shows why. Each rung is one half-life. Fifty percent done is one, seventy five percent is two, and so on up to about ten half-lives for ninety nine point nine percent.
If you prefer the formula, t equals two point three zero three over k, times log of four, which also comes out to about six hundred seconds. The shortcut and the formula agree.
Subtopic two का पहला worked example, C B S E board level. एक first-order reaction का rate constant k है two point three one into ten to the minus three per second।
Part a half-life माँगता है। First order के लिए half-life बस zero point six nine three over k है।
Plug in करो। Zero point six nine three बँटा two point three one into ten to the minus three देता है three hundred seconds. एक clean half-life।
Part b seventy five percent consume होने का time माँगता है। Seventy five percent चला जाने के बाद, reactant का एक चौथाई बचता है, और एक चौथाई मतलब दो successive halvings।
तो time है दो half-lives, दो into three hundred, यानी six hundred seconds. कोई integration नहीं चाहिए।
ये ladder बताती है क्यों। हर rung एक half-life है। Fifty percent done एक है, seventy five percent दो, और ऐसे ही ऊपर ninety nine point nine percent के लिए लगभग दस half-lives तक।
अगर formula पसंद हो, t equals two point three zero three over k, times log of four, जो भी लगभग six hundred seconds आता है। Shortcut और formula agree करते हैं।

board_events.text: Work in fractions remaining: $75\%$ complete means a quarter left $= (1/2)^2$.
$93.75\%$ complete means $6.25\%$ left $= 1/16$.
Answer: 120 minutes. The instant you see 'first order', reach for the powers-of-two ladder.

segments.text: Second example, a N E E T speed trap that rewards the ladder. A first-order reaction is seventy five percent complete in sixty minutes. When is it ninety three point seven five percent complete?
The ladder is your map. Every percentage translates into a whole number of half-lives, and then the arithmetic is trivial.
The key move for first order is to work in the fraction remaining, using fraction left equals one half raised to the number of half-lives.
Seventy five percent complete means twenty five percent remaining, which is one half squared. So that is two half-lives equal to sixty minutes, giving a half-life of thirty minutes.
Now the target. Ninety three point seven five percent complete means six point two five percent remaining, which is one sixteenth.
One sixteenth is one half to the fourth power, so that is four half-lives. Four times thirty is one hundred twenty minutes.

The answer is one hundred twenty minutes. The trap catches students who grind through the log formula twice, wasting two minutes and risking slips. The instant you see first order, reach for the powers-of-two ladder.
दूसरा example, एक N E E T speed trap जो ladder को reward करता है। एक first-order reaction साठ minute में seventy five percent complete है। ये ninety three point seven five percent कब complete होगी?
Ladder आपका नक़्शा है। हर percentage एक whole number of half-lives में translate होती है, और फिर arithmetic trivial है।
First order के लिए key move है fraction remaining में काम करना, using fraction left equals one half raised to the number of half-lives।
Seventy five percent complete मतलब twenty five percent remaining, जो one half squared है। तो वो दो half-lives बराबर साठ minute, यानी half-life तीस minute।
अब target. Ninety three point seven five percent complete मतलब six point two five percent remaining, यानी one sixteenth।
One sixteenth है one half to the fourth power, तो वो चार half-lives. चार into तीस, यानी one hundred twenty minutes।

<excited> Answer एक सौ बीस minute है। Trap उन students को पकड़ता है जो log formula दो बार grind करते हैं, दो minute बर्बाद करते हैं और slips का risk लेते हैं। जिस पल first order दिखे, powers-of-two ladder उठाओ।

sections.title: Reading Order from Half-Life Data (JEE Main)

board_events.text: JEE Main: half-life measured at two concentrations

board_events.caption: When starting concentration doubles, the half-life doubles

board_events.text: $[A]_0$ doubles and $t_{1/2}$ also doubles, so $t_{1/2}\propto [A]_0$.
It is a zero-order reaction. Now use the zero-order half-life to get $k$.
Verify with row two: $t_{1/2} = 0.20/(2\times1.25\times10^{-3}) = 80$ min. Correct.

segments.text: Third example, J E E Main, blending two skills: reading order from half-life behaviour, then extracting k. The half-life is measured at two starting concentrations.
Here is the data. At zero point one zero molar the half-life is forty minutes, and at zero point two zero molar it is eighty minutes.
Look at the pattern. When the starting concentration doubles, the half-life also doubles. So the half-life is directly proportional to the starting concentration.
Compare with the master relation, half-life proportional to starting concentration to the power one minus n. We need one minus n equal to one, so n is zero. A zero-order reaction.
Now that we know it is zero order, feed that into the matching integrated form. For zero order the half-life is the starting concentration over two k.
Using the first row, forty equals zero point one zero over two k, which gives k equal to one point two five times ten to the minus three mol per litre per minute. Notice the zero-order units.
Always verify. With the second row, zero point two zero over two times one point two five times ten to the minus three gives eighty minutes, exactly matching. The order and k are consistent.
तीसरा example, J E E Main, दो skills मिलाता है: half-life behaviour से order पढ़ना, फिर k निकालना। Half-life दो starting concentrations पर measure की गई है।
ये रहा data. Zero point one zero molar पर half-life चालीस minute है, और zero point two zero molar पर अस्सी minute।
Pattern देखिए। जब starting concentration double होता है, half-life भी double हो जाती है। तो half-life starting concentration के directly proportional है।
Master relation से compare करो, half-life proportional to starting concentration to the power one minus n. हमें one minus n बराबर one चाहिए, तो n zero है। एक zero-order reaction।
अब जब पता है कि ये zero order है, इसे matching integrated form में feed करो। Zero order के लिए half-life starting concentration over two k है।
पहली row use करके, चालीस equals zero point one zero over two k, जो देता है k बराबर one point two five into ten to the minus three mol per litre per minute. Zero-order units ध्यान दीजिए।
हमेशा verify करो। दूसरी row से, zero point two zero over two into one point two five into ten to the minus three देता है अस्सी minute, exactly matching. Order और k consistent हैं।

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: $A(g) \rightarrow 2B(g) + C(g)$, first order
