board_events.caption: Back out p_A from the measured total pressure before applying the first-order law

board_events.text: Start: pure $A$ at 0.50 atm. Let $x$ be the pressure of $A$ that reacted.

segments.text: Fourth example, J E E Advanced, testing the pressure bookkeeping trap. The gas-phase decomposition A gas gives two B gas plus C gas follows first-order kinetics.
The setup is on the board. We start with pure A at zero point five zero atmospheres, and after twenty minutes the total pressure has risen to zero point eight zero atmospheres.
Let x be the partial pressure of A that has reacted. By stoichiometry, B rises by two x and C rises by x, because their coefficients are two and one.

Add up the pressures. The total is zero point five zero minus x, plus two x, plus x, which is zero point five zero plus two x. Setting that equal to zero point eight zero gives x equal to zero point one five.
So the remaining pressure of A is zero point five zero minus zero point one five, which is zero point three five atmospheres. That is the number the rate law actually needs.

Now apply the first-order law in A's own pressure. k equals two point three zero three over twenty, times log of zero point five zero over zero point three five. Using the given log value, that is one point seven eight times ten to the minus two per minute.

Finally the half-life, zero point six nine three over k, gives about thirty eight point nine minutes. The Advanced-level catch is that the measured total pressure is not the reactant pressure, so you must back out p A first.
चौथा example, J E E Advanced, pressure bookkeeping trap को test करता है। Gas-phase decomposition A gas gives two B gas plus C gas first-order kinetics follow करती है।
Setup board पर है। हम शुरू करते हैं pure A से zero point five zero atmospheres पर, और बीस minute बाद total pressure बढ़कर zero point eight zero atmospheres हो जाता है।
Let x be A का वो partial pressure जो react हुआ। Stoichiometry से, B, two x से बढ़ता है और C, x से, क्योंकि उनके coefficients दो और एक हैं।
Pressures जोड़ लो। Total है zero point five zero minus x, plus two x, plus x, यानी zero point five zero plus two x. उसे zero point eight zero के बराबर रखने पर x बराबर zero point one five।
तो A का remaining pressure zero point five zero minus zero point one five है, यानी zero point three five atmospheres. यही वो number है जो rate law को असल में चाहिए।

अब A के अपने pressure में first-order law लगाओ। k equals two point three zero three over twenty, times log of zero point five zero over zero point three five. दिए गए log value से, वो one point seven eight into ten to the minus two per minute।

आख़िर में half-life, zero point six nine three over k, देता है लगभग अड़तीस point nine minute. Advanced-level catch ये है कि measured total pressure reactant pressure नहीं है, तो पहले p A back out करना पड़ता है।

sections.title: Common Pitfalls: Half-Life Rules, 2.303 and Pressure

board_events.text: The four traps that cost marks here
Swapping the half-life rules: first order $t_{1/2}$ is independent of $[R]_0$; zero order is proportional to it.
Mixing these two up is the single most common MCQ error in this subtopic.
Dropping the 2.303 when using base-ten logs, or pairing it with natural logs.
Pair 2.303 with $\log$ or lose the marks.
Plugging total pressure into the rate law — it needs the reactant's partial pressure.
Treating '100% completion' as finite: for first order it is asymptotic, an infinite time.
Pro-tip: translate every percentage into halvings before touching a calculator.

segments.text: Let us close subtopic two with the four traps that reliably cost marks.

First and most common, swapping the half-life rules. First order half-life is independent of the starting concentration. Zero order half-life is proportional to it. Get these backwards and the MCQ is gone.
This mix-up really is the single most common error in this subtopic, so drill it: first order forgets the start, zero order scales with the start.
Second, dropping the two point three zero three. When you use base-ten logs, the first-order constant carries that factor. Forgetting it, or pairing it with natural logs, guarantees a wrong answer.
The memory aid is simple: two point three zero three lives with log. Pair them together or lose the marks.

Third, plugging the total pressure straight into the rate law. In gas-phase problems the rate law needs the reactant's partial pressure, which you extract from the stoichiometric balance, never the measured total directly.

Fourth, treating one hundred percent completion as a finite time. For first order it is asymptotic. Each half-life removes only half of what remains, so completion is an infinite-time limit, and questions really ask about a stated fraction.

<whisper> And the pro-tip that ties it together: for first-order fraction problems, translate the percentage into halvings before you touch a calculator. Fifty is one, seventy five is two, eighty seven point five is three, ninety nine point nine is about ten.
चलिए subtopic two को उन चार traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो भरोसे से marks लेते हैं।
पहला और सबसे common, half-life rules swap कर देना। First order half-life starting concentration से independent है। Zero order half-life उसके proportional है। इन्हें उल्टा किया तो MCQ गया।
ये mix-up सच में इस subtopic की सबसे common गलती है, तो इसे drill करो: first order start भूल जाता है, zero order start के साथ scale करता है।
दूसरा, two point three zero three छोड़ देना। जब आप base-ten logs use करते हैं, first-order constant वो factor साथ रखता है। इसे भूलना, या natural logs के साथ pair करना, guaranteed गलत answer है।
Memory aid simple है: two point three zero three log के साथ रहता है। दोनों को साथ pair करो या marks खोओ।
तीसरा, total pressure को सीधे rate law में डाल देना। Gas-phase problems में rate law को reactant का partial pressure चाहिए, जो आप stoichiometric balance से निकालते हो, कभी measured total सीधे नहीं।

चौथा, one hundred percent completion को एक finite time मानना। First order के लिए ये asymptotic है। हर half-life बचे का सिर्फ़ आधा हटाती है, तो completion एक infinite-time limit है, और questions असल में एक stated fraction पूछते हैं।

<whisper> और वो pro-tip जो सब बाँधती है: first-order fraction problems के लिए, calculator छूने से पहले percentage को halvings में translate करो। पचास एक है, पचहत्तर दो, साढ़े सत्तासी तीन, ninety nine point nine लगभग दस।

sections.title: Pseudo First Order: A Reaction Wearing a Disguise

board_events.text: When a bimolecular reaction behaves as first order

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="270" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="26" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Ester hydrolysis in water</text><text x="230" y="52" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH</text><text x="230" y="92" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">true: Rate = k[ester][H₂O]</text><rect x="150" y="108" width="70" height="26" rx="4" fill="#fff8c5" stroke="#9a6700"/><text x="185" y="126" fill="#9a6700" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">[H₂O]</text><text x="255" y="126" fill="#111111" font-size="12">≈ constant (excess)</text><polygon points="222,145 238,145 230,160" fill="#333333"/><rect x="90" y="170" width="280" height="46" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="230" y="199" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Rate = k′[ester],  k′ = k[H₂O]</text><text x="230" y="245" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">observed order 1, but molecularity still 2</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Excess water is nearly constant, so it folds into the rate constant as k-prime

board_events.text: Order need not match molecularity — pseudo first order is the everyday illustration.
Picture ten wedding guests served by a kitchen stocked for a thousand.
Observed order collapses to 1, but the true molecularity is still 2.
The observed constant is $k' = k[H_2O]$ — hence 'pseudo' first order.

segments.text: In subtopic one you learned that order is experimental and need not match molecularity. Pseudo first order reactions are the most important everyday example of that gap: a genuinely bimolecular reaction that behaves, in the lab, exactly like first order.
The picture shows the trick. The true rate depends on both ester and water, but because water is in huge excess its concentration barely moves, so it quietly folds into the rate constant.
Two species react, yet only one seems to matter. That is the whole puzzle, and the resolution is about relative amounts.

<curious> Picture a small wedding with ten guests, served by a kitchen stocked for a thousand people. The guests' hunger changes dramatically, but the kitchen's stock barely drops from a thousand to nine hundred ninety.
Chemically, take the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of an ester. Ester plus water, with an acid catalyst, gives acetic acid plus ethanol.

The true rate law is second order, rate equals k times ester times water. But the reaction is run in water, so water is in enormous excess and stays effectively constant. We absorb that constant into the rate constant, giving rate equals k prime times ester.
So the observed order has collapsed to one, even though the true molecularity is still two. Two species really do collide; only the visible kinetics look first order.
That observed constant is k prime equals k times water. It carries the constant water concentration inside it, which is exactly why we call it pseudo, or fake, first order.

Subtopic one में आपने सीखा कि order experimental है और molecularity से match करना ज़रूरी नहीं। Pseudo first order reactions इसी gap का सबसे important रोज़मर्रा का उदाहरण हैं, एक genuinely bimolecular reaction जो lab में बिल्कुल first order जैसी behave करती है।
Picture trick दिखाती है। असली rate ester और water दोनों पर depend करती है, पर water इतनी बड़ी excess में है कि उसकी concentration मुश्किल से हिलती है, तो वो चुपके से rate constant में समा जाती है।
दो species react करती हैं, फिर भी एक ही मायने रखती दिखती है। यही पूरा puzzle है, और इसका हल relative amounts में छिपा है।
<curious> सोचिए एक छोटी shaadi जिसमें दस मेहमान हैं, पर kitchen हज़ार लोगों के लिए stocked है। मेहमानों की भूख बहुत बदलती है, पर kitchen का stock हज़ार से बस नौ सौ नब्बे तक गिरता है।
Chemically, ester का acid-catalysed hydrolysis लीजिए। Ester plus water, acid catalyst के साथ, देता है acetic acid plus ethanol।

असली rate law second order है, rate बराबर k times ester times water। पर reaction water में चलती है, तो water enormous excess में है और effectively constant रहती है। उसे rate constant में absorb करने पर मिलता है rate बराबर k prime times ester।
तो observed order एक तक गिर गया, जबकि true molecularity अब भी दो है। दो species सच में collide करती हैं, बस visible kinetics first order दिखती है।
वो observed constant है k prime बराबर k times water। ये constant water concentration अपने अंदर रखता है, इसीलिए हम इसे pseudo, यानी नक़ली, first order कहते हैं।

sections.title: Cane Sugar and the Isolation Method

board_events.text: A second classic, and a deliberate lab trick

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="270" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="24" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Inversion of cane sugar</text><text x="230" y="48" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → glucose + fructose</text><text x="230" y="70" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">observed Rate = k′[C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁]  (water in excess)</text><line x1="40" y1="92" x2="420" y2="92" stroke="#d0d7de" stroke-width="1"/><text x="230" y="118" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Isolation method (Ostwald)</text><rect x="40" y="132" width="380" height="90" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#8c959f"/><text x="230" y="158" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">Flood every OTHER reactant to large excess</text><text x="230" y="180" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">→ rate depends on the ONE you care about</text><text x="230" y="202" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">measure each order, then stitch the full rate law</text><text x="230" y="248" fill="#9a6700" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">a costume for k: k′ = k[excess]</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Cane-sugar inversion is pseudo first order; the isolation method generalises the idea

board_events.text: Inversion of cane sugar: sucrose plus water gives glucose and fructose.
Because it now obeys first-order kinetics, ALL the first-order machinery applies directly.
Chemists use this on purpose: flood every other reactant to isolate the one you care about.
This is Ostwald's isolation method — measure each order separately, then stitch the full rate law.

segments.text: There is a second textbook example, and then a bigger idea hiding inside it.
The picture shows both: cane-sugar inversion on top, and below it the isolation method that turns this accident into a deliberate technique.
The inversion of cane sugar: sucrose plus water, with acid, gives glucose and fructose. Again water is the excess reactant.
So the observed rate law is k prime times sucrose, first order, for exactly the same reason as the ester.

The pay-off is huge. Because the reaction now obeys first-order kinetics, every tool from subtopic two applies directly: the integrated equation, the half-life zero point six nine three over k prime, and the straight-line log plot.

And this is not just an accident of running things in water. Chemists use it on purpose. To measure the order with respect to one reactant, flood the system with large excesses of every other reactant.

That is Ostwald's isolation method. By isolating one reactant at a time under pseudo conditions, a messy multi-reactant rate law breaks into a series of simple pseudo-order experiments, and you stitch the individual orders back into the full law.
एक दूसरा textbook example है, और उसके अंदर एक बड़ा idea छिपा है।
Picture दोनों दिखाती है, ऊपर cane-sugar inversion, और नीचे isolation method जो इस accident को एक deliberate technique बना देता है।
Cane sugar का inversion, sucrose plus water, acid के साथ, देता है glucose plus fructose। यहाँ भी water excess reactant है।
तो observed rate law है k prime times sucrose, first order, बिल्कुल उसी वजह से जैसे ester में।

पे-ऑफ़ बहुत बड़ा है। चूँकि reaction अब first-order kinetics obey करती है, subtopic two का हर tool सीधे लागू होता है, integrated equation, half-life zero point six nine three over k prime, और straight-line log plot।
और ये सिर्फ़ water में चलाने का accident नहीं है। Chemists इसे जानबूझकर इस्तेमाल करते हैं। एक reactant के respect में order मापने के लिए, बाक़ी हर reactant को large excess में flood कर दीजिए।

यही Ostwald का isolation method है। एक-एक reactant को pseudo conditions में isolate करके, एक उलझा multi-reactant rate law simple pseudo-order experiments की series में टूट जाता है, और individual orders को वापस full law में stitch कर लेते हैं।

sections.title: Recognising, Reducing and Recovering

board_events.text: The three-step procedure

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="240" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="28" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Why "excess" keeps [H₂O] constant</text><text x="80" y="70" fill="#111111" font-size="13">ester reacting:</text><rect x="200" y="55" width="40" height="22" fill="#d1242f"/><text x="250" y="71" fill="#111111" font-size="12">0.02 mol</text><text x="80" y="115" fill="#111111" font-size="13">water present:</text><rect x="200" y="100" width="200" height="22" fill="#1f6feb"/><text x="200" y="145" fill="#111111" font-size="12">20 mol → 19.98 mol at full reaction</text><rect x="90" y="165" width="280" height="46" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="230" y="193" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">change ≈ 0.1% — negligible</text></svg>
board_events.caption: A little ester reacting changes the water amount by only about 0.1 percent

board_events.text: Step 1: write the true rate law, e.g. Rate $= k[A][B]$.
Step 2: identify the excess species — its concentration is nearly constant.
Step 3 (recovery): divide the observed constant by the excess concentration.
If 0.02 mol ester reacts in 20 mol water, water falls to 19.98 — a 0.1% change, negligible.

segments.text: Let us make the reasoning into a clean, repeatable procedure, plus a recovery step that examiners love.
This picture justifies the whole disguise. A tiny amount of ester reacting barely touches the mountain of water present.
Step one, write the true rate law from the genuine dependence on all reactants, for instance rate equals k times A times B.

Step two, identify the excess species, often the solvent, water. If B naught is far larger than A naught, then consuming all of A removes only a tiny fraction of B, so its concentration is essentially constant.

Step three, fold the constant in. A constant times a constant, k times B, is itself a constant, k prime, so the visible kinetics depend on A alone. Rate equals k prime times A, with k prime equal to k times B.

And there is a recovery step. Since k prime equals k times B, dividing the observed constant by the excess concentration gives back the true second-order constant, and the units shift from per second to litre per mole per second, a nice check.

Here is the numbers behind the assumption. Suppose zero point zero two mole of ester reacts in twenty moles of water. Even at complete reaction, water falls from twenty to nineteen point nine eight, a change of about one tenth of one percent. Utterly negligible, so treating water as constant is fully justified.
चलिए इस reasoning को एक clean, repeatable procedure बनाते हैं, साथ में एक recovery step जो examiners को पसंद है।
ये picture पूरे disguise को justify करती है। थोड़ा-सा ester react करना water के पहाड़ को मुश्किल से छूता है।
Step one, सभी reactants पर genuine dependence से true rate law लिखिए, जैसे rate बराबर k times A times B।

Step two, excess species पहचानिए, अक्सर solvent, water। अगर B naught, A naught से बहुत बड़ा है, तो पूरे A को consume करना B का बस एक tiny fraction हटाता है, तो उसकी concentration essentially constant है।

Step three, constant को fold कीजिए। एक constant times एक constant, k times B, ख़ुद एक constant है, k prime, तो visible kinetics सिर्फ़ A पर depend करती है। Rate बराबर k prime times A, जहाँ k prime बराबर k times B।

और एक recovery step। चूँकि k prime बराबर k times B, observed constant को excess concentration से divide करने पर true second-order constant वापस मिलता है, और units per second से litre per mole per second में shift होती हैं, एक अच्छा check।

Assumption के पीछे के numbers। मान लीजिए zero point zero two mole ester बीस moles water में react करता है। पूरे reaction पर भी water बीस से उन्नीस point नौ आठ तक गिरता है, यानी लगभग zero point one percent का change। बिल्कुल negligible, तो water को constant मानना पूरी तरह justified है।

sections.title: Confirming It Experimentally and Following It in the Lab

board_events.text: How to prove it is pseudo, not truly, first order

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="260" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="55" y1="30" x2="55" y2="150" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="55" y1="150" x2="230" y2="150" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="55" y1="150" x2="215" y2="45" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="3"/><text x="18" y="100" fill="#111111" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 18 100)">k′</text><text x="140" y="170" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">[B] excess</text><text x="120" y="70" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12">slope = k</text><text x="140" y="20" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">k′ ∝ [B]</text><rect x="255" y="40" width="175" height="115" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#8c959f"/><text x="342" y="62" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Followed in lab</text><text x="342" y="88" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">ester: titrate acid</text><text x="342" y="108" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">(V₀, Vᵗ, V∞)</text><text x="342" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">sucrose: polarimetry</text><text x="342" y="148" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">(r₀, rᵗ, r∞)</text><text x="230" y="205" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">k′ scales with [excess] ⇒ masked higher order</text><text x="230" y="228" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">a true first-order k′ would NOT depend on [B]</text></svg>
board_events.caption: k-prime rises linearly with the excess concentration; lab methods track a physical property

board_events.text: Vary the excess reactant at fixed limiting reactant, and measure $k'$ each time.
Ester hydrolysis is followed titrimetrically — titrate the acid produced.
A genuinely first-order reaction shows NO dependence on $[B]$; only a masked one does.

segments.text: How do you actually prove a reaction is pseudo first order rather than truly first order? The test is elegant.
The graph is the heart of it: plot the observed constant against the excess concentration. A straight line through the data is the fingerprint of a disguise.
Hold the limiting reactant fixed and vary the excess reactant. Measure the observed constant k prime at each excess concentration.

Now test whether k prime equals k times B. If k prime scales linearly with the excess concentration, the reaction is pseudo first order. Only a masked higher-order reaction carries the excess concentration inside its observed constant.

Because the limiting reactant is often hard to titrate directly, these reactions are tracked through a physical property. Ester hydrolysis is followed titrimetrically: the acid produced is titrated against standard alkali at intervals.
In that form, the first-order equation uses alkali volumes. k prime equals two point three zero three over t, times log of the quantity V infinity minus V zero, over V infinity minus V t.

Sucrose inversion is followed polarimetrically, because sucrose is dextrorotatory while the product mixture is net laevorotatory. The same law becomes k prime equals two point three zero three over t, times log of r zero minus r infinity, over r t minus r infinity.
The clinching point: a genuinely first-order reaction shows no dependence on the excess concentration. Only a masked higher-order reaction does, so the linear k prime versus excess plot settles it.
आप असल में कैसे साबित करें कि reaction pseudo first order है, न कि truly first order? Test elegant है।
Graph ही इसका दिल है, observed constant को excess concentration के against plot कीजिए। Data में से एक सीधी line disguise का fingerprint है।
Limiting reactant fixed रखिए और excess reactant vary कीजिए। हर excess concentration पर observed constant k prime measure कीजिए।

अब test कीजिए क्या k prime बराबर k times B। अगर k prime excess concentration के साथ linearly scale करता है, तो reaction pseudo first order है। सिर्फ़ एक masked higher-order reaction excess concentration को अपने observed constant के अंदर रखती है।

चूँकि limiting reactant अक्सर सीधे titrate करना मुश्किल है, इन्हें एक physical property से track करते हैं। Ester hydrolysis titrimetrically follow होती है, बनी acid को standard alkali के against अंतराल पर titrate करते हैं।
उस form में first-order equation alkali volumes use करती है। k prime बराबर two point three zero three over t, times log of the quantity V infinity minus V zero, over V infinity minus V t।

Sucrose inversion polarimetrically follow होती है, क्योंकि sucrose dextrorotatory है जबकि product mixture net laevorotatory। वही law बनता है k prime बराबर two point three zero three over t, times log of r zero minus r infinity, over r t minus r infinity।
निर्णायक बात, एक genuinely first-order reaction excess concentration पर कोई dependence नहीं दिखाती। सिर्फ़ masked higher-order दिखाती है, तो linear k prime versus excess plot मामला तय कर देता है।

sections.title: Pseudo First Order: Definitions and Working Formulas

board_events.text: The consolidated pseudo-first-order toolkit
Definition: a truly higher-order reaction whose observed order is 1 because one reactant is in large excess.

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="180" fill="#ffffff"/><rect x="30" y="55" width="150" height="60" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#d1242f"/><text x="105" y="80" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">Rate = k[A][B]</text><text x="105" y="102" fill="#d1242f" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">true, order 2</text><text x="215" y="80" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">[B] ≈ const</text><polygon points="195,88 245,88 245,82 260,92 245,102 245,96 195,96" fill="#333333"/><rect x="280" y="55" width="150" height="60" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37"/><text x="355" y="80" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">Rate = k′[A]</text><text x="355" y="102" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">observed, order 1</text><text x="230" y="150" fill="#9a6700" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">k′ = k[B],  recover k = k′/[B]</text></svg>
board_events.caption: The second-order rate law reduces to first order; recover k from k-prime

board_events.text: Observed $k'$ has units per second; the true $k = k'/[B]$ is in litre per mole per second.
Diagnostic: molecularity $= 2$ (theoretical), observed order $= 1$ (experimental).

segments.text: Let us gather the pseudo-first-order toolkit in one place for quick reference.

The definition first: a pseudo first order reaction is one whose true, higher order reduces to an observed order of one, because one reactant is present in such large excess that its concentration stays effectively constant.
The reduction, in symbols. Rate equals k times A times B; with B approximately constant, this becomes k prime times A, where k prime equals k times B.
The picture shows the two ends: a true second-order law on the left, an observed first-order law on the right, with k prime equals k times B linking them.

Because it is now first order, the tools carry over unchanged. k prime equals two point three zero three over t, times log of A naught over A, and the half-life is zero point six nine three over k prime.
Mind the units. The observed k prime is in per second, first-order units. The true k, recovered as k prime divided by the excess concentration, is in litre per mole per second.

And the diagnostic to remember: the molecularity is two, the theoretical count of colliding species, while the observed order is one, the experimental value. This is the cleanest real example of order not equalling molecularity.
चलिए pseudo-first-order toolkit को quick reference के लिए एक जगह इकट्ठा करते हैं।

पहले definition, pseudo first order reaction वो है जिसका true, higher order एक observed order तक घट जाता है, क्योंकि एक reactant इतनी large excess में है कि उसकी concentration effectively constant रहती है।
Reduction, symbols में। Rate बराबर k times A times B; B के approximately constant होने पर ये बनता है k prime times A, जहाँ k prime बराबर k times B।
Picture दोनों छोर दिखाती है, बाईं तरफ़ true second-order law, दाईं तरफ़ observed first-order law, और k prime बराबर k times B दोनों को जोड़ता है।
चूँकि अब ये first order है, tools unchanged carry over होते हैं। k prime बराबर two point three zero three over t, times log of A naught over A, और half-life zero point six nine three over k prime।
Units का ध्यान रखिए। Observed k prime per second में है, first-order units। True k, k prime को excess से divide करके recover होता है, litre per mole per second में है।

और वो diagnostic जो याद रखना है, molecularity दो है, colliding species का theoretical count, जबकि observed order एक है, experimental value। ये order not equal to molecularity का सबसे साफ़ real example है।

sections.title: Methyl Acetate Hydrolysis: Half-Life and 90% (CBSE)

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="270" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="26" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Ester hydrolysis in water</text><text x="230" y="52" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH</text><text x="230" y="92" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">true: Rate = k[ester][H₂O]</text><rect x="150" y="108" width="70" height="26" rx="4" fill="#fff8c5" stroke="#9a6700"/><text x="185" y="126" fill="#9a6700" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">[H₂O]</text><text x="255" y="126" fill="#111111" font-size="12">≈ constant (excess)</text><polygon points="222,145 238,145 230,160" fill="#333333"/><rect x="90" y="170" width="280" height="46" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="230" y="199" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Rate = k′[ester],  k′ = k[H₂O]</text><text x="230" y="245" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">observed order 1, but molecularity still 2</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Water in excess makes the hydrolysis behave as first order

board_events.text: (a) Water is the solvent, in large excess, so $[H_2O]$ is constant and folds into $k'$.
(b) For 90% hydrolysed, a tenth of the ester remains.
Once it is first order, reuse every first-order result unchanged.

segments.text: First worked example of subtopic three, C B S E board level. The acid-catalysed hydrolysis of methyl acetate is pseudo first order with observed rate constant k prime equal to four point six two times ten to the minus three per minute.
The picture reminds us why: water is the excess partner, so its concentration hides inside k prime and the reaction reads as first order.

Part a asks why it is pseudo first order. The true rate law is k times ester times water, but water is the solvent and in large excess, so its concentration stays essentially constant. Absorbing it gives rate equals k prime times ester, first order.

Now the half-life. For first order it is zero point six nine three over k prime, which is zero point six nine three over four point six two times ten to the minus three, giving one hundred fifty minutes.
Part b, ninety percent hydrolysed. That leaves one tenth of the ester, so the concentration ratio A naught over A is ten.
Apply the formula. t equals two point three zero three over k prime, times log of ten. Log of ten is one, so t is about four hundred ninety eight minutes.
The lesson: the moment you recognise pseudo first order, you reuse every first-order result unchanged, no new machinery required.

Subtopic three का पहला worked example, C B S E board level। Methyl acetate का acid-catalysed hydrolysis pseudo first order है, observed rate constant k prime बराबर four point six two into ten to the minus three per minute।
Picture याद दिलाती है क्यों, water excess partner है, तो उसकी concentration k prime के अंदर छिप जाती है और reaction first order पढ़ी जाती है।

Part a पूछता है ये pseudo first order क्यों है। True rate law है k times ester times water, पर water solvent है और large excess में, तो उसकी concentration essentially constant रहती है। उसे absorb करने पर मिलता है rate बराबर k prime times ester, first order।
अब half-life। First order के लिए ये zero point six nine three over k prime है, यानी zero point six nine three over four point six two into ten to the minus three, जो देता है एक सौ पचास minutes।
Part b, ninety percent hydrolysed। इससे ester का one tenth बचता है, तो concentration ratio A naught over A दस है।
Formula apply कीजिए। t बराबर two point three zero three over k prime, times log of ten। Log of ten एक है, तो t लगभग चार सौ अट्ठानवे minutes।
सबक़, जिस पल आप pseudo first order पहचानें, हर first-order result unchanged reuse कर लीजिए, कोई नई machinery नहीं चाहिए।

sections.title: Which Statement Is Correct? (NEET)

board_events.text: NEET: ethyl acetate hydrolysis in dilute acid

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="210" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="26" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Ethyl acetate hydrolysis</text><rect x="40" y="45" width="170" height="120" rx="10" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="125" y="70" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Molecularity</text><text x="125" y="100" fill="#111111" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">2</text><text x="125" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">ester + water</text><text x="125" y="148" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">collide</text><rect x="250" y="45" width="170" height="120" rx="10" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="2"/><text x="335" y="70" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Observed order</text><text x="335" y="100" fill="#111111" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">1</text><text x="335" y="130" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">k′ = k[H₂O]</text><text x="335" y="148" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">water hidden in k′</text><text x="230" y="195" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">the cleanest example of order ≠ molecularity</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Molecularity stays 2 while observed order is 1 — the cleanest split

board_events.text: Molecularity counts colliding species: ester and water make 2, so 'molecularity 1' is wrong.
The observed order is 1 because water is constant, so 'observed order 2' is wrong.
Water is folded into $k'$, so it does not appear in the observed rate law.
Correct answer: the observed constant DOES depend on the water concentration.
Trap: seeing 'first order' and assuming molecularity is 1, or treating $k'$ as truly constant.

segments.text: Second example, a N E E T speed trap. The hydrolysis of ethyl acetate in dilute aqueous acid is pseudo first order, and you must pick the correct statement.
This contrast is the whole answer: molecularity two on one side, observed order one on the other, cleanly separated.
First, molecularity counts the species that collide: ester and water, so two. Any option claiming molecularity one is wrong.
Second, the observed order is one, because water is held constant by its excess. So any option claiming observed order two is wrong.
Third, water is folded into k prime, so it does not appear explicitly in the observed rate law. That rules out the option saying water appears in the observed law.
What is left is the key relationship: k prime equals k times water.
So the correct statement is that the observed constant does depend on the water concentration, through k prime equals k times water. That dependence is the signature of the disguise.

The trap catches students who see first order and assume molecularity is one, or who treat k prime as a true constant independent of everything. Remember: observed order one, molecularity unchanged, and k prime carries the hidden excess.
दूसरा example, एक N E E T speed trap। Ethyl acetate का dilute aqueous acid में hydrolysis pseudo first order है, और आपको correct statement चुनना है।
ये contrast ही पूरा जवाब है, एक तरफ़ molecularity दो, दूसरी तरफ़ observed order एक, साफ़-साफ़ अलग।
पहला, molecularity collide करने वाली species गिनती है, ester और water, तो दो। Molecularity एक कहने वाला कोई option ग़लत है।
दूसरा, observed order एक है, क्योंकि water अपनी excess से constant रखी जाती है। तो observed order दो कहने वाला option ग़लत है।
तीसरा, water k prime में fold हो जाती है, तो वो observed rate law में explicitly नहीं आती। इससे वो option रद्द होता है जो कहता है water observed law में आती है।
जो बचता है वो key relationship है, k prime बराबर k times water।
तो correct statement ये है कि observed constant water concentration पर depend करता है, k prime बराबर k times water के ज़रिए। यही dependence disguise का signature है।

Trap उन्हें पकड़ता है जो first order देखकर molecularity एक मान लेते हैं, या k prime को हर चीज़ से independent true constant समझ लेते हैं। याद रखिए, observed order एक, molecularity unchanged, और k prime hidden excess रखता है।

sections.title: Recovering the True Rate Constant (JEE Main)

board_events.text: JEE Main: from $k'$ back to the true $k$

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="190" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="30" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Recover true k from k′</text><text x="230" y="66" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">k = k′ / [H₂O] = (2.0×10⁻³) / 55.5</text><rect x="120" y="85" width="220" height="42" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="230" y="112" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">= 3.6×10⁻⁵ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹</text><text x="230" y="160" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">units shift s⁻¹ ÷ mol L⁻¹ → L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹: a self-check</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Dividing k-prime by the water concentration recovers the true second-order k

board_events.text: Water is essentially constant at 55.5 mol per litre; observed $k' = 2.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1}$.
Dividing per second by mol per litre gives litre per mole per second.
The unit change is a dimensional self-check that the conversion is sound.

segments.text: Third example, J E E Main. For the ester hydrolysis with true rate law k times ester times water, we recover the true second-order constant from the observed one.
The picture shows the single move and, importantly, the unit shift that comes with it.
We are told water is essentially constant at fifty five point five moles per litre, and the observed pseudo first order constant is two point zero times ten to the minus three per second.
Since k prime equals k times water, we invert: k equals k prime divided by the water concentration, which is two point zero times ten to the minus three, over fifty five point five.
That gives three point six times ten to the minus five litre per mole per second.
Look at the units. Dividing per second by moles per litre gives litre per mole per second, exactly the second-order units.
That unit change is the multi-concept catch and a built-in self-check. If the units did not land on second-order units, the conversion would be wrong.
तीसरा example, J E E Main। Ester hydrolysis के लिए, true rate law k times ester times water के साथ, हम observed constant से true second-order constant recover करते हैं।
Picture single move दिखाती है और, ज़रूरी बात, उसके साथ आने वाला unit shift।
हमें बताया गया है water essentially constant है पचपन point पाँच moles per litre पर, और observed pseudo first order constant है दो point zero into ten to the minus three per second।
चूँकि k prime बराबर k times water, हम invert करते हैं, k बराबर k prime divided by water concentration, यानी दो point zero into ten to the minus three, over पचपन point पाँच।
इससे मिलता है तीन point छह into ten to the minus five litre per mole per second।
Units देखिए। Per second को moles per litre से divide करने पर मिलता है litre per mole per second, बिल्कुल second-order units।
वो unit change multi-concept catch है और एक built-in self-check। अगर units second-order units पर न बैठतीं, तो conversion ग़लत होता।

sections.title: Half-Life That Ignores [A]-nought but Tracks [B] (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: two observations, one explanation

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="210" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="28" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Half-life of A under excess B</text><text x="230" y="62" fill="#111111" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">t½ = 0.693 / (k[B])</text><text x="60" y="100" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12">independent of [A]₀</text><text x="60" y="125" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="12">∝ 1/[B]: double [B] → half the t½</text><rect x="90" y="140" width="280" height="46" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2"/><text x="230" y="169" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">k = 0.693/(t½·[B]) = 3.0×10⁻² L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Half-life is independent of [A]0 but inversely proportional to [B]

board_events.text: (a) Under excess $B$, $A$ decays by first order, so $t_{1/2}$ does not contain $[A]_0$.
(b) At $[B] = 0.50$ the half-life is 46.2 s; solve for the true $k$.
The observed half-life is tunable through $[B]$ — proof that $k'$ is composite, not fundamental.

segments.text: Fourth example, J E E Advanced, and it ties the whole subtopic together. A reaction A plus B, with true rate law k times A times B, is studied under excess B. The half-life of A is independent of A naught but halves when B doubles.
The picture states both facts at once: t one half does not contain A naught, yet it is inversely proportional to B.

Part a explains both. Under excess B, the rate is k prime times A with k prime equal to k times B, so A decays by first order and its half-life, zero point six nine three over k prime, contains no A naught. Hence independence of the starting amount.

But k prime equals k times B, so the half-life is zero point six nine three over k times B, which is proportional to one over B. Doubling B doubles k prime and halves the half-life. Both observations are pure pseudo first order signatures.
Part b, put in numbers. At B equal to zero point five zero moles per litre, the measured half-life is forty six point two seconds.

Solve for the true k. From half-life equals zero point six nine three over k times B, k equals zero point six nine three over the product of zero point five zero and forty six point two, which is three point zero times ten to the minus two litre per mole per second.

The deep point: the true constant k is fixed, but the observed half-life is tunable through the excess concentration. That is a clean demonstration that k prime is a composite quantity, not a fundamental constant.

चौथा example, J E E Advanced, और ये पूरे subtopic को जोड़ देता है। एक reaction A plus B, true rate law k times A times B के साथ, excess B में study होती है। A का half-life A naught से independent है पर B के double होने पर आधा हो जाता है।
Picture दोनों facts एक साथ बताती है, t one half में A naught नहीं है, फिर भी वो B के inversely proportional है।

Part a दोनों समझाता है। Excess B में rate है k prime times A, जहाँ k prime बराबर k times B, तो A first order से decay करता है और उसका half-life, zero point six nine three over k prime, में कोई A naught नहीं। इसलिए starting amount से independence।

पर k prime बराबर k times B, तो half-life है zero point six nine three over k times B, जो one over B के proportional है। B double करने पर k prime double और half-life आधा। दोनों observations pure pseudo first order signatures हैं।
Part b, numbers डालिए। B बराबर zero point five zero moles per litre पर, measured half-life है छियालीस point दो seconds।

True k के लिए solve कीजिए। Half-life बराबर zero point six nine three over k times B से, k बराबर zero point six nine three over the product of zero point five zero and छियालीस point दो, यानी तीन point zero into ten to the minus two litre per mole per second।
Deep point, true constant k fixed है, पर observed half-life excess concentration से tunable है। ये साफ़ दिखाता है कि k prime एक composite quantity है, कोई fundamental constant नहीं।

sections.title: Pseudo First Order: Pitfalls and Pro-Tips

board_events.text: Four traps and one reflex
Saying molecularity is 1 because it is 'first order' — pseudo changes only the observed order.
Molecularity, for example 2 for ester hydrolysis, is unchanged.
Treating $k'$ as fundamental — it is $k' = k[\text{excess}]$; change the excess and $k'$ changes.
Only $k$ is intrinsic. Observed $k'$ is per second; the true $k$ is in litre per mole per second.
Forgetting the excess requirement — deplete the 'excess' reactant and true second-order returns.
Reflex: any hydrolysis 'in water' or 'acid-catalysed' described as first order — suspect pseudo.
Tag the excess species, fold it into $k'$, and reuse every first-order result from subtopic two.

segments.text: Let us close subtopic three with four traps and one useful reflex.
First, the big one: saying molecularity is one just because the reaction is first order. Pseudo first order changes only the observed order.
The molecularity is untouched. For ester hydrolysis it is two, because ester and water genuinely collide.
Second, treating k prime as a fundamental constant. It is k prime equals k times the excess concentration. Change the excess and k prime changes with it.
Only k is intrinsic. And watch the units: the observed k prime is in per second, while the true k, recovered as k prime over the excess, is in litre per mole per second.
Third, forgetting the excess requirement. The first-order disguise holds only while the excess reactant is barely consumed. Deplete it appreciably and the true second-order behaviour returns.
Here is the reflex to build. Whenever a hydrolysis in water, or an acid-catalysed reaction, is described as first order, suspect pseudo first order.

Then just tag the excess species, fold it into k prime, and reuse every first-order result from subtopic two unchanged: the half-life zero point six nine three over k prime, the log plot, and the completion ladder.
चलिए subtopic three को चार traps और एक useful reflex के साथ बंद करते हैं।
पहला, बड़ा वाला, molecularity एक कह देना सिर्फ़ इसलिए कि reaction first order है। Pseudo first order सिर्फ़ observed order बदलता है।
Molecularity untouched है। Ester hydrolysis के लिए ये दो है, क्योंकि ester और water सच में collide करते हैं।
दूसरा, k prime को fundamental constant मानना। ये है k prime बराबर k times excess concentration। Excess बदलिए तो k prime भी बदलता है।
सिर्फ़ k intrinsic है। और units का ध्यान, observed k prime per second में है, जबकि true k, k prime over excess के रूप में recover, litre per mole per second में।
तीसरा, excess requirement भूल जाना। First-order disguise तभी तक टिकता है जब तक excess reactant मुश्किल से consume हो। उसे appreciably deplete करें तो true second-order behaviour लौट आता है।
और वो reflex जो बनाना है, जब भी कोई hydrolysis water में, या acid-catalysed reaction, first order बताई जाए, pseudo first order का शक कीजिए।

फिर बस excess species tag कीजिए, k prime में fold कीजिए, और subtopic two का हर first-order result unchanged reuse कीजिए, half-life zero point six nine three over k prime, log plot, और completion ladder।

sections.title: Why Warming Speeds Things Up: Collision Theory

board_events.text: Two filters every collision must pass

Orientation</text><text x="335" y="104" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">must be aimed</text><text x="335" y="124" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">the right way</text><text x="335" y="158" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">energetic but</text><text x="335" y="176" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">mis-aimed fails</text><text x="230" y="232" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">like a baraat handshake: bump AND face each other</text></svg>
board_events.caption: An effective collision needs both enough energy and the right orientation

board_events.text: Rule of thumb: the rate roughly doubles for every 10 degree Celsius rise.
Yet 10 degrees raises the average molecular speed by only a few percent — something else is going on.
Collision theory: molecules are hard spheres that must collide to react, but not every collision works.
Filter one, energy: the collision must carry at least the activation energy $E_a$.
Filter two, orientation: even an energetic collision fails if the molecules are pointed the wrong way.
Only collisions passing both filters are effective and make product.

segments.text: Everyday life already tells you that warming things up speeds chemistry: milk sours in a day on the counter but lasts a week in the fridge. Let us understand why the dependence is so steep.
The picture names the two conditions a collision must meet: enough energy, and the right orientation.
For over a century chemists have used a rough rule: the rate roughly doubles for every ten degree Celsius rise.
Here is the remarkable part. A ten degree rise raises the average molecular speed by only a few percent, yet the rate can double. So mere speeding-up cannot be the whole story.
Collision theory models molecules as hard spheres that must collide to react. But, crucially, not every collision works. Two filters apply.

The first is an energy filter. The colliding molecules must carry at least a minimum energy, the activation energy E a, to break old bonds and start forming new ones. Softer collisions just bounce apart.
The second is an orientation filter. Even an energetic collision fails if the molecules are pointed the wrong way.

<chuckle> Think of a crowded baraat where guests must shake hands to react. They have to actually bump into each other, and be facing the right way with hands out. Only collisions passing both filters are effective and make product.
रोज़मर्रा की ज़िंदगी पहले ही बता देती है कि warming चीज़ों को तेज़ करता है, दूध counter पर एक दिन में खट्टा, पर fridge में हफ़्ता भर चलता है। चलिए समझें ये dependence इतनी steep क्यों है।
Picture दो conditions नाम लेती है जो एक collision को पूरी करनी हैं, पर्याप्त energy, और सही orientation।
एक सदी से chemists एक rough rule इस्तेमाल करते हैं, rate हर दस degree Celsius rise पर मोटे तौर पर double हो जाती है।
यहाँ remarkable बात है। दस degree का rise average molecular speed को बस कुछ percent बढ़ाता है, फिर भी rate double हो सकती है। तो सिर्फ़ speeding-up पूरी कहानी नहीं हो सकती।
Collision theory molecules को hard spheres मानती है जिन्हें react करने के लिए collide करना होता है। पर, ज़रूरी बात, हर collision काम नहीं करती। दो filters लगते हैं।

पहला energy filter है। Colliding molecules को कम-से-कम एक minimum energy, activation energy E a, carry करनी होगी, ताकि पुराने bonds टूटें और नए बनने लगें। Softer collisions बस bounce करके अलग हो जाती हैं।
दूसरा orientation filter है। एक energetic collision भी fail हो जाती है अगर molecules ग़लत दिशा में हों।

<chuckle> एक भरी baraat सोचिए जहाँ मेहमानों को react करने के लिए हाथ मिलाना है। उन्हें सच में एक-दूसरे से टकराना है, और सही तरफ़ हाथ बढ़ाए हुए face करना है। सिर्फ़ दोनों filters पास करने वाली collisions effective हैं और product बनाती हैं।

sections.title: The Maxwell-Boltzmann Tail, Arrhenius, and Catalysts

board_events.text: Where the temperature mystery dissolves

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="270" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="55" y1="30" x2="55" y2="220" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="55" y1="220" x2="435" y2="220" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><text x="20" y="140" fill="#111111" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 20 140)">fraction of molecules</text><text x="230" y="255" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">kinetic energy</text><path d="M55,220 C110,60 150,55 200,120 C250,185 330,210 420,218" fill="none" stroke="#1f6feb" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="150" y="70" fill="#1f6feb" font-size="12">T₁ (lower T)</text><path d="M55,220 C120,120 180,110 240,150 C300,185 360,200 420,210" fill="none" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="270" y="130" fill="#1a7f37" font-size="12">T₂ (higher T)</text><line x1="330" y1="30" x2="330" y2="220" stroke="#d1242f" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="336" y="48" fill="#d1242f" font-size="12">Eᵢ</text><text x="230" y="240" fill="#9a6700" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">higher T swells the tail beyond Eᵢ</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Raising temperature broadens the distribution and swells the fraction beyond Ea

board_events.text: Molecular energies are spread across a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution — most middling, a few very energetic.
The total area is fixed; raising $T$ flattens the peak, shifts it right, and fattens the high-energy tail.
$E_a$ sits out on the tail, so a modest temperature rise swells the reacting fraction dramatically.
The term $e^{-E_a/RT}$ is the fraction with energy at least $E_a$; $A$ folds in collision frequency and orientation.
A catalyst offers a lower-$E_a$ path — it leaves $\Delta H$ and the equilibrium untouched.

segments.text: Now the temperature mystery dissolves, and it hinges on one picture.
This is the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. The taller blue curve is a lower temperature; the flatter green curve, shifted right, is a higher temperature with a much fatter high-energy tail.
At any temperature, molecular energies are spread across this distribution. Most molecules have middling energy, a few are sluggish, and a small tail are very energetic.

Two features matter. The total area under the curve is fixed, because it is the whole population. And when you raise the temperature, the peak flattens and shifts right, and the curve broadens, so proportionally many more molecules populate the high-energy tail.

The activation energy sits out on that tail. Because raising the temperature swells the fraction beyond E a far faster than it raises the average energy, even a modest temperature rise gives a large rate increase.
This is captured by the single most important relationship of the subtopic, the Arrhenius equation: k equals A times e to the minus E a over R T.
The term e to the minus E a over R T is precisely the fraction of molecules with energy at least E a. The factor A folds in how often molecules collide and how often they are correctly oriented.

A catalyst works by a completely different route: it offers an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction can clear the now-lower barrier. Crucially it does not touch the reactant or product energies, so delta H and the equilibrium position are unchanged, and it speeds forward and backward equally.
अब temperature का rahasya सुलझता है, और ये एक picture पर टिका है।
ये Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution है। ऊँची blue curve lower temperature है, और flatter green curve, दाईं तरफ़ shifted, higher temperature है जिसकी high-energy tail बहुत fatter है।
किसी भी temperature पर, molecular energies इस distribution में फैली होती हैं। ज़्यादातर molecules की energy middling है, कुछ sluggish हैं, और एक छोटी tail बहुत energetic है।

दो features मायने रखती हैं। Curve के नीचे का total area fixed है, क्योंकि वो पूरी population है। और temperature बढ़ाने पर peak flatten और दाईं तरफ़ shift होता है, curve broaden होती है, तो proportionally बहुत ज़्यादा molecules high-energy tail में आ जाते हैं।
Activation energy उसी tail पर बैठी है। चूँकि temperature बढ़ाना E a से आगे वाला fraction, average energy से कहीं तेज़ी से swell करता है, एक modest temperature rise भी बड़ा rate increase देता है।
यही capture होता है subtopic की सबसे important relationship, Arrhenius equation में, k बराबर A times e to the minus E a over R T।
Term e to the minus E a over R T ठीक-ठीक वो fraction है जिनकी energy कम-से-कम E a है। Factor A समेटता है कि molecules कितनी बार collide करते हैं और कितनी बार सही oriented होते हैं।

<excited> Catalyst बिल्कुल अलग रास्ते से काम करता है, वो एक lower activation energy वाला alternative pathway देता है, तो ज़्यादा बड़ा fraction अब कम barrier पार कर लेता है! पर वो reactant या product energies को नहीं छूता, तो delta H और equilibrium position unchanged रहते हैं, और forward व backward दोनों को बराबर तेज़ करता है।

sections.title: Derivation: The Two-Temperature Arrhenius Form

board_events.text: Eliminating $A$ using two temperatures

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="230" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="60" y1="25" x2="60" y2="185" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="185" x2="420" y2="185" stroke="#333333" stroke-width="2"/><text x="30" y="110" fill="#111111" font-size="13" transform="rotate(-90 30 110)">ln k</text><text x="240" y="215" fill="#111111" font-size="13">1 / T</text><line x1="80" y1="50" x2="390" y2="165" stroke="#1a7f37" stroke-width="3"/><text x="200" y="90" fill="#d1242f" font-size="13">slope = −Eᵢ/R</text><text x="70" y="45" fill="#111111" font-size="12">intercept = ln A</text></svg>
board_events.caption: ln k against 1/T is a straight line of slope minus Ea over R

board_events.text: $\log A$ is the same at both temperatures, so subtracting eliminates it.
Sign check: with $T_2 \gt T_1$, the bracket is positive, so $k_2 \gt k_1$ — higher $T$, larger $k$.

segments.text: Let us derive the two-temperature Arrhenius form, the workhorse for finding activation energy.
Its graphical cousin is on the board: natural log of k against one over T is a straight line whose slope is minus E a over R.
Start from the logarithmic Arrhenius equation written at two temperatures. Log k one equals log A minus E a over two point three zero three R T one, and log k two is the same with T two.
The key observation: log A is temperature-independent, so it is identical at both temperatures. Subtracting the two equations eliminates it entirely.
What remains is log of k two over k one equals E a over two point three zero three R, times the quantity one over T one minus one over T two.

Do a sign check, worth memorising. With T two greater than T one, the bracket one over T one minus one over T two is positive, so k two is greater than k one. Higher temperature, larger rate constant, as it must be.

Combining the fractions gives the exam-standard form: log of k two over k one equals E a over two point three zero three R, times the quantity T two minus T one, over T one T two. This is what you use to extract E a from two rate-constant measurements.
चलिए two-temperature Arrhenius form derive करते हैं, activation energy निकालने का workhorse।
इसका graphical cousin board पर है, natural log of k को one over T के against एक सीधी line है जिसकी slope minus E a over R है।
Logarithmic Arrhenius equation दो temperatures पर लिखकर शुरू कीजिए। Log k one बराबर log A minus E a over two point three zero three R T one, और log k two वही T two के साथ।
Key observation, log A temperature-independent है, तो दोनों temperatures पर बिल्कुल एक जैसा है। दोनों equations को घटाने पर वो पूरी तरह eliminate हो जाता है।
जो बचता है वो है log of k two over k one बराबर E a over two point three zero three R, times the quantity one over T one minus one over T two।

एक sign check कीजिए, याद रखने लायक़। T two के T one से बड़े होने पर, bracket one over T one minus one over T two positive है, तो k two, k one से बड़ा है। Higher temperature, larger rate constant, जैसा होना चाहिए।

Fractions जोड़ने पर exam-standard form मिलता है, log of k two over k one बराबर E a over two point three zero three R, times the quantity T two minus T one, over T one T two। यही आप दो rate-constant measurements से E a निकालने के लिए use करते हैं।

sections.title: Derivation: The Boltzmann Fraction and the Steric Factor

board_events.text: Why the energy term is a Boltzmann fraction

board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="460" height="200" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="28" fill="#111111" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Rate = P · Z₊₋ · e⁻ᴴᵀₒᴸᵗ</text><rect x="30" y="55" width="120" height="70" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#8c959f"/><text x="90" y="80" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">Z₊₋</text><text x="90" y="102" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">collision</text><text x="90" y="118" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">frequency</text><rect x="170" y="55" width="120" height="70" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#d1242f"/><text x="230" y="80" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">e⁻ᴴᵀₒᴸᵗ</text><text x="230" y="102" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">energy</text><text x="230" y="118" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">fraction ≥ Eᵢ</text><rect x="310" y="55" width="120" height="70" rx="8" fill="#f6f8fa" stroke="#1a7f37"/><text x="370" y="80" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">P</text><text x="370" y="102" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">steric factor</text><text x="370" y="118" fill="#111111" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">orientation</text><text x="230" y="165" fill="#111111" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">Compare with Arrhenius: A = P · Z₊₋</text><text x="230" y="188" fill="#9a6700" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">P ≤ 1 corrects for orientation</text></svg>
board_events.caption: Collision frequency times energy fraction times orientation gives the rate

board_events.text: $Z_{AB}$ counts collisions per unit time and volume, but only the energetic fraction reacts.
From the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, that fraction is exactly $e^{-E_a/RT}$.
Comparing with Arrhenius identifies $A$ with the collision frequency.
Real molecules also need orientation, so we insert the steric factor $P \le 1$.

segments.text: Now let us see why the exponential term in Arrhenius is a Boltzmann fraction, and where the steric factor comes from.
The picture breaks the collision-theory rate into three pieces: how often molecules collide, what fraction have enough energy, and what fraction are correctly aimed.
The collision-theory rate for a bimolecular reaction is written as Z A B times e to the minus E a over R T.
Here Z A B counts how many collisions occur per unit time per unit volume. But only the fraction carrying energy at least E a can actually react.
From the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, that reacting fraction is exactly e to the minus E a over R T. This is the same exponential that appears in Arrhenius.
Comparing the two expressions, k equals A times e to the minus E a over R T, identifies the pre-exponential factor A with the collision frequency.

But the theory still over-predicts for real molecules, because it ignores orientation. So we insert a steric factor P, which is at most one, correcting for the fraction of energetic collisions that also happen to be correctly oriented.

The corrected rate is P times Z A B times e to the minus E a over R T. Comparing with Arrhenius now gives A equals P times Z A B: the pre-exponential factor bundles both collision frequency and orientation.
अब देखते हैं कि Arrhenius में exponential term एक Boltzmann fraction क्यों है, और steric factor कहाँ से आता है।
Picture collision-theory rate को तीन हिस्सों में तोड़ती है, molecules कितनी बार collide करते हैं, कितने fraction के पास पर्याप्त energy है, और कितने fraction सही aimed हैं।
Bimolecular reaction के लिए collision-theory rate लिखी जाती है Z A B times e to the minus E a over R T।
यहाँ Z A B गिनता है कि per unit time per unit volume कितनी collisions होती हैं। पर सिर्फ़ वो fraction जो कम-से-कम E a energy carry करता है, असल में react कर सकता है।
Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution से, वो reacting fraction ठीक e to the minus E a over R T है। यही exponential Arrhenius में आता है।
दोनों expressions compare करने पर, k बराबर A times e to the minus E a over R T, pre-exponential factor A को collision frequency से identify करता है।

पर theory अब भी real molecules के लिए over-predict करती है, क्योंकि वो orientation ignore करती है। तो हम steric factor P डालते हैं, जो अधिकतम एक है, energetic collisions के उस fraction को correct करता है जो सही oriented भी हों।
Corrected rate है P times Z A B times e to the minus E a over R T। अब Arrhenius से compare करने पर A बराबर P times Z A B, pre-exponential factor collision frequency और orientation दोनों को समेटता है।

board_events.text: Reading the energy-versus-coordinate diagram
